Mr. Speaker, in response to questions on October 26 and 27 the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) undertook to make a statement today concerning the federal-provincial conferences and the meetings of the tax structure committee that were held last week. Because of a minor throat ailment the Prime Minister has asked me to make the statement today on his behalf.
The more important federal statements made at the conference have already been distributed to hon. members in both languages and can be tabled officially if so desired later today. I should like to ask, Mr. Speaker, whether I have permission when we have gathered the documents together in both languages to have them tabled later today.

speechtext:
On Monday, Tuesday and the first part of Wednesday, October 24, 25 and 26, the conference concerned itself with the rapidly increasing needs of higher education in Canada which are imposing so great and growing a burden upon the provincial governments. The talks of last week showed very clearly that all jurisdictions in Canada are vitally concerned to play their full part in strengthening the educational system at all levels. Such action will foster the nation's growth, will enable Canada to play its full part in the world of today, and most important of all will enrich the lives of young Canadians.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
The federal government recognizes that it must assist in providing the financial resources needed for the general support of our institutions of post-secondary education. In the light of this recognition, proposals were put forward by the federal government to assist the provinces through a special arrangement of fiscal transfers related in
amount to the operating costs for postsecondary education in Canada. The plan would replace the present university grants program and much of the assistance for technical and vocational training under the current agreements which expire next March.
In the conference there was agreement with the principles underlying the new arrangement and with the concept that the transfer, though taking into account the costs of higher education, should be unconditional and designed to exert no influence on the structure and content of provincial programs. Differences of view were expressed as to the amount of the transfer and the manner in which it should be calculated. There was, as expected, difficulty in finding an acceptable definition of post-secondary education, one that would recognize the diversity of present educational systems and at the same time be equitable in relation to all provinces. Subject to settling this definition and that of "operating costs", the amount of the federal fiscal transfer to be recommended to parliament will be based on 50 per cent of postsecondary operating costs. Taking into account the recommendations of the Bladen Commission and the universities we would regard this as a suitable contribution now toward both the operating costs of institutions of higher education, and the capital costs of buildings and equipment. An optional measure is proposed, amounting to $15 per capita, which would expand in proportion to the growth in the total operating costs of post-secondary education in Canada generally-
The new arrangements would take into account the expiry on March 31, 1967, of the agreements under which operating and capital grants have been paid in respect of vocational high schools, technological institutes, trade schools and other facilities for technical and vocational training. Several provinces were strongly of the view that the proposals first made by the federal government for transitional arrangements in respect of capital grants were inadequate and did not take into account commitments they had made in the expectation that the agreements would be continued. After the government considered the provincial views on this matter, the Prime Minister proposed on October 26 that
October 31, 1966

Federal-Provincial Conference the transitional arrangements should provide that capital grants would be available, without limit as to time, for the purposes covered by the present agreements, until they had reached, for each province, $800 per capita of its population aged 15 to 19 as of 1961. For Canada as a whole some $548 million in capital grants will remain available over a period of years after next March 31.
We must recognize that rapid technological and industrial change now require more and more training and re-training of adults. This is of fundamental importance if full employment and increased productivity are to be achieved. The federal government has a responsibility for ensuring that the required training is financially possible for people in the labour force.
For this purpose, the federal government proposes to pay training allowances directly to adults who are taking occupational training, in place of sharing provincial costs as we are now doing. The federal government will also purchase the necessary training services on behalf of these adults from provincial training institutions and from industry, wherever suitable occupational training facilities are to be found. We will thus meet the full costs of such training.
Our proposal was to define an adult as one who has been three years out of school and in the labour force. Several of the provinces felt this was unduly restrictive. We undertook to discuss immediately with the provinces whether some modified definition is possible which would meet more of the training needs of people who have been in the labour force for less than three years, while still preserving the important distinction between this training program and the school system.
We believe that the federal government's proposals for financing the costs of higher education and for the training of the labour force provide a sound foundation on which federal and provincial governments can discharge their respective responsibilities. By facilitating the expansion in education facilities and increasing the amount of training in respect of the labour force, our proposals will help greatly to ensure expanding and equal economic opportunities for people in all parts of Canada.
On Wednesday, Thursday and the beginning of Friday, October 26, 27 and 28, the tax structure committee met for the fifth time following its establishment by the Federal-Provincial Conference of 1964. The committee gave further intensive consideration to the

fiscal questions that had been referred to it, including proposals that I made to the fourth meeting on September 14, 1966. The views presented to the tax structure committee, and the committee's discussions, were communicated to the federal-provincial conference to assist it in reviewing the matters it had referred to the committee.
The conference later accepted a recommendation from the tax structure committee that it should be authorized to sit again during 1967 and 1968. The principal purpose of these further meetings will be to discuss the implications for federal and provincial tax laws of the reports of the federal and provincial royal commissions and committees on taxation, and to consider again in that context the use of tax fields by the federal, provincial and municipal governments.
The conference proceeded on October 28 to review the federal fiscal proposals in their entirety. The federal government's proposals relating to the equalization and stabilization of provincial revenues met with a substantial measure of approval. None of the provinces decided to accept at this time the proposal which I made on September 14, 1966 relating to the possible transfer to the provinces of 17 points of personal income tax, with accompanying equalization payments, to cover the costs of established and continuing shared-cost programs in the health and welfare fields already covered in the case of Quebec under the Established Programs Act.
With regard to the sharing of tax fields, the premiers of all the provinces took the position that was to be expected: they expressed strongly the view that the needs of the provinces required the transfer of substantially more tax resources to the provinces than was proposed by the federal government.
The Prime Minister and I explained the considerations which made it impossible for the federal government further to abate federal personal and corporate income taxes at this time, for reasons that have been given in the published federal statements. After much serious discussion, the conference recognized that it was not possible to arrive at a tax sharing arrangement which could be regarded as fully satisfactory to both the federal and provincial governments.
New tax collection agreements to prevail for two years were discussed and will be proceeded with. During that time substantial
October 31. 1966

adjustments will have to be considered in the light of the decisions taken by governments following the consideration of the reports of the royal commissions and committees on taxation to which I have already referred.

speechtext:
I think it will cover all the specific questions that were asked of the Prime Minister on October 26 with regard to the changes resulting from the new proposals. I should make clear that it has been necessary in preparing this table to estimate the amount that should be excluded from the present grants as covering the costs of adult training, which the federal government is proposing to assume directly. Because of the way the records have been kept it is necessary to estimate these amounts after endeavouring to forecast how many will be covered by the new definition of adult.
The total of the financial transfers to the provinces in this year 1966-67 under the present equalization arrangements and existing grants for universities and technical and vocational training comes to approximately $623 million. The parallel arrangements proposed for next year, 1967-68, after making the necessary and difficult adjustments which flow from the changes in the nature of the arrangements proposed, come to $973 million-an increase of about $350 million or over 50 per cent in a single year. There is no magical way to transfer funds like this: they have to be found either from reductions in other federal programs or by getting higher revenues. It was a measure of the federal government's concern for higher education that it was prepared to vacate four points of personal income taxes and one point of corporate income tax to make it easier for the provinces to secure the revenues they require. We did not feel that we could go further than this.
These figures I have cited do not include the costs of adult training which the government intends should be expanded vigorously. The assumption of the full cost of this program by the federal government will also add to our expenditures next year.
In 1966-67, equalization payments are expected to total $353 million. In 1967-68 under the new proposals they are forecast to reach $547 million-an increase just short of $200 million. These equalization payments account for far the largest part of the $350 million increase to which I have already referred.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, and this will not come as any great surprise to hon. members, may I say that the main area of disagreement was one, and one alone-money. To have expected agreement on this complex and controversial subject would be naive. We believe that the results were sound and they

will, both in the immediate future and in the long term, redound to the advantage of Canadians generally.
Hon. members of course will have several opportunities to debate these matters as legislation is brought forward to implement the proposals.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the report of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) on this very important dominion-provincial conference is long and, in some respects, detailed. Just by listening to the report one cannot make a completely detailed answer but I do think that certain salient points come to a head in his report. The first deals with education.
After the report of the Bladen commission-the Bladen group, which was arranged for by the Association of Universities, supported by the Ford Foundation-and after the report of the Canada Council last fall, one would have thought that the warning lights would be on the show that education must be recognized as a national need, requiring the highest priority in Canada at this time of her industrial development if we are to compete successfully in the modern international race for markets.
But what has happened? Just listening to the minister's report one sees where the provincial governments have been given a small number of corporation tax and personal income tax points, from which they will be required to meet the fantastically rapid increasing costs of education. With the tremendous pressure on provincial governments to meet the costs not only of higher education but of all levels of education, one can understand why the provinces left this meeting very unhappy or, as somebody has said, equalized in unhappiness.
I would think, Mr. Speaker, that the attitude of all federal parties should be that, regardless of past positions taken by them on the subject of education vis-a-vis the federal government and the provinces, the time has now come to accept the fact that in the national interest the federal government will have to play an increasingly larger part in the field of education. This I say without intent whatsoever to interfere with the rights of the provinces in their control over the subject matter of education at the elementary and secondary levels.
I simply point out that all parties, 100 years after we signed the original B.N.A. Act, have to accept the fact that education is no
October 31, 1966	COMMONS
longer purely a provincial matter. The federal government must take part in the training of our people to meet the challenges of the century ahead, and therefore it is a question of devising the formulae whereby we can help without interfering with provincial rights.
I would suggest that the training of staff for the universities, research at universities, which is very expensive, the plant itself, and the per capita grant system all offer combinations to produce a formula that would not interfere with the provinces' rights to control the educational content, but I submit this opportunity was missed by turning over more of the resources of the federal government to the provinces and saying, "You do it; you take on the worries". On the contrary the national need requires much more joint effort not less. I would gather that the provincial premiers and treasurers felt, following this meeting, that they have been left alone to carry this burden.
The second point I want to make, Mr. Speaker, is that on this question of control over education one thing that seemed to be forgotten at this dominion-provincial conference was that the universities themselves are objecting more and more strenuously not only to the impending control that there might be from the federal government but also to the fact that more and more provinces are interfering with the educational functions of our universities.
Our universities can produce this free frontier type thinking only when they are free not only from federal but also from provincial interference as well. I think some thought should have gone into introduction of some formula whereby more money could go into higher education, with hands off by both the federal and provincial governments. There are precedents for this.
The third point I should like to make has to do with the shared cost programs. From the experience of the last three years when we have seen the federal government backing up and backing up under the pressures from strong provincial governments, I know it is natural for us in this federal house to applaud a government which says, "all right, take over the shared program and we will give you more money". But this omits and forgets the essential fact that we in the federal parliament do have responsibility for this whole nation and for good government of this whole nation, and should be reluctant at all times to give away our power or initiative. This in effect is what has been going on.

I do not think this is a matter for division on a partisan basis. I see it simply as a trend which can be very dangerous to Canada if we have to face either the serious menace of recession or the serious menace of outside pressure. In an effort to make all provinces equal I suggest that this tendency to turn over the initiative of the federal government can put us in a strait-jacket in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I will confine my remarks to the educational aspect of the minister's statement. He did not tell us very much about the tax structure committee and the recommendations of that committee. The different proposals concerning university education will satisfy no one. The provincial premiers have gone away unhappy because they have not got as much money as they wanted. The Canadian universities are unhappy that the federal government seems to be withdrawing from this field altogether. The president of the University of British Columbia deplored the fact that the federal government is withdrawing from the field of university education. The case for provincial control over elementary and secondary education may be quite clear, but I suggest there is a very great deal of doubt concerning secondary education at universities in particular. We feel there is a place for federal leadership here.
As the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) has pointed out, the universities will be completely under the control of their respective provinces, quite apart from the fact that they should expect federal leadership in this field. There will be general disagreement that the government is phasing itself out of the field of technical and vocational education. The only part of the program with which we find satisfaction is that concerning adult or technical education. This is a broad field and the government should play a useful role here. On the question of higher education, particularly at the universities, the problems facing the universities in Canada in respect of research and graduate training will not be solved on an individual provincial basis. The 10 systems might be quite different. There is a real need for federal leadership here. Provincial premiers notwithstanding, and provincial autonomy notwithstanding, a large number of people expect the federal government to play a role here without taking over the lower levels of education.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we listened very attentively to the statement made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) about the federal-provincial conference held last week here in Ottawa.
The minister spoke quite frankly when he said that the general disagreement between the federal government on the one hand and the provinces on the other was of a financial nature. Everyone thought of it, everyone heard about it; not a single premier went home satisfied with the outcome of that federal-provincial conference which finally ended in failure, something we have come to expect in all the years that those federal-provincial conferences have been held.
No doubt this caused the premier of the province of Quebec to say that the Ottawa Minister of Finance was not diplomatic enough, whereas the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) was too diplomatic. And from that statement one concludes that the Prime Minister was conciliatory and the Minister of Finance was not or is not.
Mr. Speaker, education was discussed the whole week. In the field of education, the provinces want to keep their autonomy, their independence and their right to decide. Today, the Minister of Finance told us that all the provinces are asking the federal government to contribute more and more to education while respecting provincial autonomy. Not later than last night, the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development (Mr. Sauve) who attended the whole conference last week said: Because the provinces do not want to increase taxes, they are asking the federal government to assume responsibility for it and since the latter will have to pay $350 million more per year to the provinces, it is normal that it will have to increase taxes and, therefore, impose heavier fiscal or financial burdens on the Canadian taxpayers.
Mr. Speaker, I would like the Minister of Finance to tell us very clearly this afternoon which of the provincial premiers suggested, for instance, to the federal government that the services of the Bank of Canada be used to finance education in the provinces, education for the young as well as adults, to find the financial means without increasing taxes? Which of the provincial premiers suggested to the Minister of Finance to adapt the financial system to Canada's needs and not to impose on Canadians additional burdens which they cannot assume at this time? The hon. Minister of Finance is aware of that.

DEBATES	October 31. 1966
Mr. Speaker, it is all very' well to be told, here, on the morrow of a week-long conference, that the whole problem was nothing but financial, that all the provincial representatives, as well as the hon. Minister of Finance and the right hon. Prime Minister, discussed monetary matters without, however, attempting to modify the system and adapting it to the conditions and needs of 1966.
We were told, even before the conference, that the Quebec premier had given the hon. Minister of Finance the following ultimatum: Give us 100 per cent of personal and corporate income tax or else we may have to secede from the rest of Canada. Was it mentioned last week? Certainly not, nobody ever mentioned it.
Mr. Speaker, education is one of the most important matters that have been discussed last week and I will remind the Minister of Finance that the education of our youth, and to a lesser degree adult education is of the utmost importance.
During my visit to Russia last year, I had the opportunity to find out that university students were paid 35 rubles per month to continue and complete their studies. This takes place in Russia, a communist country. And what does it mean?
Students are given a presalary without any obligation, except that they probably have to be true communists, so as to allow them to carry on their studies.
But I would like to call the minister's attention to the following point: If, in a communist country, a government can manage to pay salaries to students, why is it that in countries like ours that claim freedom of choice and democracy, we do not have the means to help our university students by paying them a presalary while they are attending university or high school?
Mr. Speaker, this matter is serious enough to make governments ponder, especially those that are called free governments or governments respecting private enterprises. I feel that if socialists and communists can do it, we too can do it by taking advantage of the means at our disposal, namely the Bank of Canada, instead of continually turning to the United States and begging permission to do what we are able to do here ourselves. Mr. Speaker, I believe we have had enough of this manoeuvring and these proposals which, in the end, are meaningless.
October 31, 1966

I do not wish to delay the house any longer but, before concluding with my comments, I insist it is time the hon. Minister of Finance stop fooling and going against the provinces. He and the government should concentrate on putting the Bank of Canada at the disposal of the Canadian citizens and then, the conflict which exists at present between the provinces and the federal government would disappear; the provinces would be respected and the federal government would be fulfilling its purpose. This is what the Creditistes and the Social Credit party have been claiming all over Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the length of time required for the negotiations which have led up to this statement of the Minister
of Finance (Mr. Sharp), and considering its great importance it would have been preferable had each official party in the opposition been given a copy of it. We are faced with a considerable burden in replying immediately to a statement of this length and importance.
Having regard to the disposition of funds to universities I think it important that we do not lose sight of the fact that universities should have several sources of funds. These sources should not all be governmental. One source is by tradition the fees, and another is through gifts by people who are interested in a university and wish to see it progress.
I am afraid this is one area of university revenue that has tended to dry up in these last few years, owing to the onerous tax burdens that are being placed on so many of the citizens of this country.
We welcome the additional aid in grants for the adult training programs but we think that this action is belated. The federal government could well have moved into this particular area earlier and the adult training programs could have proceeded at a faster pace than at present.
It is difficult to make a comment at the present time, on the fiscal proposals because of their complex nature, which has baffled many experts and has also baffled the people who write newspaper headlines over the past week. I understand the premier of British Columbia is quoted as saying that that province held its own and that this constituted a victory for the province. 2.	In respect to each ship, what are the names, home ports, functions and which ones are fitted with LORAN?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Byrne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):

speechtext:
1. Sixteen Canadian Coast Guard ships usually operate in the Eastern Arctic in the summer months.
2. The names of Canadian Coast Guard ships which operate in the Eastern Arctic are given below with their current home ports although basing arrangements are changed from time to time. Seven of these ships are fitted with LORAN and this is denoted by an asterisk following the ship's name.
Quebec city, Que.: C.C.G.S., d'Iberville*;
C.C.G.S., N.B. McLean*-, C.C.G.S., Montcalm*; C.C.G.S., Simon Fraser; C.C.G.S., CD. Howe*; C.C.G.S., Eider; C.C.G.S., Puffin; C.C.G.S., Raven; C.C.G.S., Skua. Dartmouth,
[Mr. Bell (Carleton).)
N.S.: C.C.G.S., John A. Macdonald*; C.C.G.S., Labrador*; C.C.G.S., Narwhal*; C.C.G.S., Auk; C.C.G.S., Gannet. Charlottetown, P.E.I.: C.C.G.S. Wolfe. St. John's, Nfld.: C.C.G.S., Sir Humphrey Gilbert.
All above C.C.G. ships carry a full cargo of supplies northbound for the various Arctic posts, and they also carry some cargo and equipment on their return trip south. They are available for search and rescue duty and one or more may at any time be directed by the coast guard rescue officer to render assistance if loss of life is imminent.
The various functions of these ships while in the Arctic after discharge of northbound cargo may be summarized as follows:
The C.C.G.S. John A. Macdonald, d'Iberville, Labrador, N. B. McLean, Montcalm, Wolfe and Sir Humphrey Gilbert are icebreakers and support the Eastern Arctic sealift mainly by assisting through ice government chartered ships and others, including C.C.G. ships which are not icebreakers. The N. B. McLean, assisted by other icebreakers as necessary, is assigned to the Churchill route and helps commercial shipping by providing icebreaker assistance and advice on the best route to follow to and from Churchill. One heavy icebreaker remains in the Arctic as late as conditions permit to carry out ice formation studies in an effort to determine the latest date to which shipping may safely venture in these regions.
The C.C.G.S. Narwhal is a depot ship and provides accommodation and technical assistance for the stevedores who unload the ships at the various posts in the Fox Basin and along the East Baffin coast.
The C.C.G.S. Eider, Puffin, Raven, Skua, Auk, Gannet are known as northern supply vessels and are shallow draft carriers; their main function after discharging is to lighten cargo vessels including tankers. These ships also move cargo from Churchill to posts in the Hudson Bay and Strait. On their return trip they carry landing craft and other heavy equipment which may have to be brought south for repair.
The C.C.G.S. Simon Fraser does not normally take part in the sealift and her main function is to put into commission all light and radio beacon stations in the Hudson Bay and Strait before the opening of the Churchill route for commercial shipping each year. These aids to navigation are maintained during the shipping season but are decommissioned after the last commercial ship has sailed the route outward.

The proportions requested in this resolution, which will be succeeded by a bill, are intended to provide for all necessary requirements of the public service up to November 30, 1966.
In no instance is the total amount of any item being released by this resolution or the bill which is to follow. The form of the resolution and of the subsequent bill is the usual one for interim supply resolutions and bills. The passing of this resolution and the succeeding bill will not prejudice the rights and privileges of members to criticize any item of the estimates not yet passed when it comes up for consideration in committee of supply, and the usual undertaking is hereby given that such rights and privileges will be respected and will not be curtailed or restricted in any way as a result of the passing of this measure.
I would further explain that what is asked for in this resolution, and in the succeeding bill, is interim supply to the end of November, 1966, that is, for one month's supply with a few exceptions which are outlined in the resolution. All the other items for which more than one-twelfth is requested total less than $34 million.

The request by the government for interim supply makes it possible for us to discuss important matters with which the house has not had an opportunity to deal

for a considerable length of time. I think the most important of these matters is the whole question of defence, particularly the plan and the course the minister has been following to implement the proposed unification of our three armed services.
For more than two years now, there has been steadily increasing concern and alarm over the state of our armed forces. During that period the numbers of servicemen in our forces have decreased at an alarming rate. Morale is extremely low. Defence installations of all kinds have been closed down. The number of naval ships in commission has been cut by some 50 per cent. Confusion and disorganization has been apparent in several commands and in the administrative organization.
Finally, this summer, nearly all the more senior officers who had not already left the service resigned or were dismissed, indicating that they could not continue to support and carry out the minister's plan for the complete unification of the forces, and that their advice was being disregarded or ignored. Great confusion and uncertainty exists both on the part of the general public and on the part of those who have been active in defence matters as to what the present situation in the defence department actually is, and what it is likely to be in the future if the minister's plans are carried forward.
Many experienced ex-servicemen and students of military matters are concerned that the minister and the government have no clear ideas as to the aims of military policy, or that their aim is merely to run down our military forces until they are capable only of carrying out certain international peace activities on behalf of the United Nations.
It cannot be too strongly emphasized that the very sovereignty and independence of Canada depend on our maintaining efficient and effective defence forces capable of protecting our land area, our coastal waters and our air space against easy encroachment. We need forces capable of mobilizing our maximum national capacity in the event of war, forces capable of discharging our responsibilities and commitments to our allies in NATO and NORAD, and capable of meeting the demands made on them by the United Nations.
Members of this house, and the Canadian public, have the right to know whether the plans of the minister will produce such forces. We do not know this now, and much of the available evidence indicates that we

are likely to end up with forces which cannot discharge any of these responsibilities effectively-even that of support to the United Nations.
I think it is not generally realized how essential it is for Canada to have effective defence forces if we are to continue to receive a great deal of the information which is vital to the decisions we have to make constantly in the fields of international affairs and defence matters, and if we are to continue to have an opportunity to influence the policies of our allies in the western alliance and exert any real influence on decisions on world affairs. Without effective defence forces, the weight we can exert in these spheres must be very greatly diminished.
The minister is a great propagandist. Since taking office he has had his publicity machine operating at full speed ahead at all times in an effort to persuade the Canadian public that everything was as well as ever as far as the defence department is concerned. In particular, he has tried to gain support for his policies by maintaining he was saving the taxpayers large sums of money-always a popular line to follow. This claim has no foundation whatever, but I am sorry to say it has fooled a large number of people, including some newspaper reporters and editors.
To show that the claim is false, all one needs to do is to examine the figures as they appear in the estimates and the public accounts for the past four or five years. An examination of this table will show that in 1962-63, the last year the Conservative party was in office, expenditures totalled $1,571 million in round figures. I am leaving out the odd hundreds of thousands, although these are given in each case in the table. The estimates for 1963-64, prepared whilst I was minister, provided for expenditures of $1,590 million. The Liberal government actually spent $1,683 million in that year, an increase of $93,465,000 over our estimate, and $112,437,000 more than we spent in the previous year. In other words, there was a large increase in expenditures of $112 million in the first year that this minister and his government were responsible for defence expenditures.
At the same time as this was going on, the minister was declaiming practically every month that he was saving the taxpayers large amounts of money. That is a measure of the reliability which we can place on many of the statements he makes. In 1964-65 the minister did succeed in bringing down expenditures as compared with the previous year. The estimate was for $1,525 million. He spent $10 million more than that, a total of $1,535 million, which was some $35 million less that we spent during the last year we were in office. However, in 1965-66 expenditures were up to $1,561 million, an increase of some $26 million over the previous year, and $10 million less than was spent in 1962-63.
The estimate for the present year, 1966-67, is for expenditures of $1,572 million, an increase of $11 million. But, Mr. Chairman, the actual expenditure will be much higher than that because of the special pay for pilots which has been instituted and because of the general pay increase, as well as other things along that line which have been sanctioned. Thus a large sum will have to be added to the figures given in our estimates.
These figures show conclusively that, rather than saving the taxpayers money, during the

period this government has been in office it has spent on the average some $22 million a year more than was spent during the last year we were in office, and to be added to that is the as yet unknown but large increase for the present year.
But more important even than this, Mr. Chairman, is the fact that while this increase in expenditures has been taking place, our military strength and effectiveness have seriously declined. We have 20,000 fewer men in the services. We have a 50 per cent decrease in naval ships in commission. We have closed a large number of military installations, thus reducing our capability and potential. In addition a state of disorganization and low morale is prevailing. In other words, Mr. Chairman, the Canadian public is paying more for defence and getting much less of it.
The return on our defence dollar has been drastically reduced. I only trust that the minister will not continue to make the totally unsubstantiated claim that he is saving the taxpayers money. The figures prove conclusively that his conduct of affairs has cost the taxpayers more money, and at the same time the amount of return which the public has received on each dollar paid for defence has been very much reduced.
The minister has proceeded much further toward his goal of unification of the forces than he has any parliamentary mandate to go, and has done so against the advice of the senior officers of the department who were in the best position to know whether such moves were wise or practical. The amendment to the Defence Act passed by parliament provided for the abolition of the chiefs of staff of the navy, the army and the air force, and the vesting of their powers in one chief of defence staff. But the act still provided for a navy, an army and an air force.
Thus we have the situation where the minister received parliamentary authority for integration of the staffs and administrative functions, but he did not receive any mandate for unification of the services. He has been attempting to go ahead with that unification in spite of the fact there has been no parliamentary approval for it, and in effect has been attempting to present us with a fait accompli.
This brings up the question of the difference between integration and unification, something which has always been very much blurred by the minister. The result has been that the majority of the public think of these

two things as being exactly the same. The two terms are quite often used synonymously.
In this connection, I understand there was a television program yesterday on which three officers from the three forces, with their backs turned to the camera, were asked various questions about integration and expressed themselves in favour of integration. But nothing was said about unification. The whole objective of the program was to try to continue blurring the difference between integration and unification, to persuade the general public that these were one and the same thing; that these three officers and other officers in the armed services were all in favour of the moves which the minister is making, something which is very far from being the case as the numerous resignations, dismissals and refusals to re-engage have indicated.
Integration means in effect the bringing together of certain staffs, certain command functions, and certain administrative functions into single organizations. Integration is something which has been going on in the armed services for many years. A good deal of it had taken place before the minister took office, and I think nearly every one has been in favour of a certain amount of integration. On numerous occasions I have expressed myself as fully in favour of the integration of the administrative functions of the services, such as a single vehicle repair and maintenance organization, a single chaplains service which we have had for years, a single medical service, a single pay service, and so on.
Everyone has approved this sort of thing, and everyone did so because it was integration of a type that was practical and feasible. Now, the minister has attempted to take that approval on the part of most people to be approval for unification, which is a totally different thing. Unification means the abolition of the three separate forces, the navy, the army and the air force, and throwing them all into one pot.
To begin with, the minister apparently believed for some time, judging by the answers he gave in the house and the statements he made outside it, that you could put all the forces together into one organization and then detail people from it, no matter what their background might have been, to do any job which happened to be open in the new force. Apparently he believed that you could put a man trained in the army into the navy, a man trained to do an army job into the air force, and vice-versa.

He learned that this was neither a practical nor a possible sort of operation. We now have had from him statements that the fighting units of the navy, army and air force will be retained and that they must continue to carry on in much the same way they always have carried on. Well, under these circumstances what is the purpose in trying to throw them into one organization? What is to be gained by putting them all into one uniform, and so on? The fact is that no valid evidence has been put forward by the minister or by anyone else, either military or financially, to substantiate such a course. On the other hand, nearly all the men of long military experience and knowledge to whom I have spoken have stated that the proposed unification will further reduce morale and result in ineffective forces unable to meet our defence needs. Surely, under these circumstances, this major change should not be proceeded with until all the best evidence available has been brought before us and all the probable results and implications have been made clear. The only way this can be done is by submitting the entire unification question to our committee on national defence so that members of that committee may hear evidence from all those who know what the present situation is, and who are best qualified to inform us what will be the results of the minister's proposed plans.
Since this session resumed we have been attempting to have this action taken. The government has been adamant in refusing to follow this course. One must ask why? Are they afraid to have the facts brought out? The course of concealment followed by the minister would indicate that this is the situation. The house and the Canadian people, however, have a right to know the facts in respect of this whole situation. We must ask under what pretext can any responsible government refuse to have these facts brought out in the only way this can be done, that is by having a full investigation by the national defence committee or by a royal commission. There are just the two alternatives. One or the other course I think must be followed. Until one of these courses is followed there should be a complete halt to the unification plans and activities of the minister.
I call upon the Prime Minister to accept his responsibility in this extremely important matter and to authorize a full investigation immediately in one of the two ways I have mentioned. The minister has said the matter

will be referred to the committee on national defence after the bill he proposes to introduce to amend the Defence Act to provide for unification has had second reading. This is not good enough. Once second reading has been given, the minister will say that parliament has approved unification and there is no point in the national defence committee questioning that decision, and therefore no point in the committee bringing forth evidence to show that the decision might be wrong or completely unwise. Once more, of course, in this case the minister quite evidently is trying the tactic of fait accompli. He is trying to muzzle the committee in order to prevent it being effective. The only reasonable course to follow is for the committee to go into the whole matter before the bill is given second reading. Otherwise, members will not know what they are voting for when they are faced with this bill. In effect, they will be asked to buy a pig in a poke. Because this gas can be transmitted more cheaply and it will be delivered at cheaper cost to the consumer.
On what do you base that statement?

This statement is based on the reports of the Conservation Board of Alberta and the National Energy Board. It is not based on a speech made on the hustings.
Above all, Mr. Chairman, exports to the United States markets would provide added volume which would significantly lower transportation costs. The National Energy Board states that the United States route would lower transmission costs by 5 per cent. The consumer, of course, must benefit, and I agree with that. It is the responsibility of the National Energy Board and the various utility boards to make certain that Canadians benefit. It is spelled out in the act that the National Energy Board must always protect the nation and the people in the nation. That is their function and their jurisdiction.
We have an outstanding staff on the National Energy Board of this country. They are able, learned and experienced; and above all they are Canadians. The board has made a decision. If the Great Lakes pipe line plan had not been approved, at the very least this would have meant a loss of firm export sales
Interim Supply
of 170 million cubic feet per day to the American Natural Gas Company and its affiliates in the U.S. market. In ten years this would represent a loss of $194 million.
But this, Mr. Chairman, is only a very small part of the story. The plan now approved will open up United States markets not yet really determinable but estimative, just as the trans-Canada railway, the C.P.R., opened up the great bread basket of the world in western Canada. Wheat today is a $2 billion industry. In petroleum and natural gas we have a $1 billion industry. Let us not kill it with narrow issues and narrow politics. In this regard I will stake the policies of Alberta against the policies of Saskatchewan prior to 1963.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, our national oil policy, worked out by the Conservative government and carried out by this government, would be in jeopardy if we failed to export natural gas.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
What do I mean by that? After the Suez crisis was over we ran into a situation of difficulty with respect to our export of crude petroleum. We then realized that petroleum was coming into eastern Canada from the United States and if quotas were implemented with respect to the United States, gasoline prices to the consumer in Ontario and Quebec would have increased. Rather than do this-and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, the former minister of agriculture, had something to do with this as had the Minister of Trade and Commerce-we worked out a deal whereby the northwestern states together with Canada's domestic market took something like 800,000 barrels of crude petroleum per day. We reached that target; 800,000 barrels per day were either exported or used in Canada's domestic market.
What is the United States going to say, when this has been worked out. This is a very sensitive situation. Can we say that there will be no gas for export? These things have to be worked out by mutual understanding, mutual agreement, for our mutual benefit. We are not in the nineteenth century; this is the twentieth century.
North America's trade relations in oil and gas have been painstakingly built on the basis of mutual respect and confidence between the United States and Canada. We have a deal to hold the large portion of the northwestern United States market while the

October 31. 1968
Interim Supply
United States holds a large portion of our eastern market. This has existed since the Conservative government implemented the National Oil Policy in 1959. As a result, our sales of crude petroleum from western Canada to the United States have more than tripled.
Remember, Mr. Chairman, there were strong political pressures in the United States against this. I think the hon. member for Medicine Hat mentioned the pressures in the United States against this deal being given to Canada. Does any thinking government, or any thinking member of the opposition want to destroy that mutual confidence in our petroleum industry which exists today between Canada and the United States for the benefit of both nations? Is this not a matter to weigh carefully, when we are considering Canada's interests?
We move our crude petroleum from the west to Ontario via the United States. Why is it so dangerous or inimical to Canada's sovereignty to move natural gas in the same fashion, when one remembers that we have such a plentiful surplus for export. We went to bed with our coal in western Canada. Should we go to bed with our natural gas? My answer is no. And why did we lose our coal markets? Because, I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, narrow minded politicians masqueraded under the guise of "Canada first". Today our coal towns are ghost-like. Such a thing should not happen to the petroleum industry of western Canada.
How is it going to sit with the United States when we ask them to allow more imports of Canadian oil? It will not sit very well. What are the United States independents going to say when El Paso Natural Gas and Pacific Gas and Electric ask the Federal Power Commission later this year for authorization to increase their imports of Canadian gas by some 400 million cubic feet per day? How do we counter the argument that the United States consumers should not rely on foreign gas regulated by a foreign government?
The future success of our growing billion dollar a year oil and gas industry is heavily dependent on the freedom of access to the fuel hungry United States markets, just as the future success of our $2 billion per year wheat industry depends on the human hunger of the world, even if those hungry humans live behind the iron curtain.
[Mr. Woolliams.l
If it is right to trade with Communists, it is certainly right to trade with the United States for natural gas. Canada, without trade, and without transmission pipe lines carrying her raw materials to the markets cannot hope to reach the destiny which Laurier predicted when he said that "The twentieth century will be ours".
This plan is good for British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario, and will mean cheaper production to southern Ontario where the population exists, and where the heart of Canada's industry lies. Let not the members of the New Democratic Party use Ontario for their arguments, because their arguments hold no water so far as Ontario is concerned.
Does any line go to southern Ontario?
The line will carry sufficient to supply its industrial needs.
They are supplied now.
You are forgetting about the export market, as you forget about coal out of western Canada. Where is your argument?
Nonsense.
I do not want to get into an argument. The hon. member is very sensitive because he does not like to listen to hon. members from other parties.
I have not heard any arguments.

If the hon. member opens his ears he might-remember lend me your ears.
We control the flow of gas. We control the source as effectively as we control the land which produces the wheat and cattle. The New Democratic Party, by their definition of Canada's sovereignty, are living in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Their thinking has not expanded with the moving times.
Today a nation must give up some power and some freedom to obtain more power and more freedom, and to maintain economic independence.
In summary-and I see that my time is almost up-I have eight points, if the committee will hear me. I have eight reasons to show why our national interest is protected, and why the National Energy Board was correct in the stand it took. What are those
October 31, 1966

reasons? First of all, we have a huge surplus of natural gas. Let the New Democratic Party deny that. Second, we have the original all-Canada route. It does not matter whether it is a 30 inch pipe or a 36 inch pipe. The amount of gas that moves through any pipe line is based on the pressure through the pipe line, and not on the circumference of the pipe.
But is pressure not limited?

The United States route will bring a large part of the flow back into Canada.
Third, northern Canada has all the gas it needs. The south and the export market must be considered. That is, northern Canada has its supply. Fourth, Canada always controls the system, as she controls the amount of the flow of gas. In addition, she regulates the United States' use of the gas.
Fifth: foreign ownership will probably be accelerated by the refusal to approve the routes. In other words, there will be less money for Canadians to invest. It must be remembered that we have a $2 billion a year wheat industry, and a $1 billion a year petroleum industry.
Sixth: the gross national product will not grow with underdeveloped resources. We need to develop our resources. We do not want to do with this industry what happened with coal in Saskatchewan. We do not want to leave our natural gas in the ground.
That is not so.
The hon. member does not like to hear the facts. I challenge the hon. member to ascertain the facts in Saskatchewan as compared with Alberta. I challenge him to examine the facts-
Nonsense.
We will not listen to the hon. member's nonsense any more.
He is talking tommyrot.

The hon. member says I am talking tommyrot. It is he who has always talked a lot of rot, but his name is Tommy Douglas.
Seventh, our foreign earnings will be increased to exports, and this in turn will lessen our dependency on foreign capital. Eighth, and this is my final point, we have one all-Canadian route, and this new plan will add to our own supply, particularly

when one examines the undertakings and assurances made by Trans-Canada to the energy board.
In conclusion I say this: that we have a surplus of natural gas. The plan decided on by the National Energy Board is a proper plan. It was approved by the governor in council according to law and it means much to the economy of western Canada. It means much to the economy of Canada, when one considers our imbalance of trade with the United States which my good friends to the left are the first to crow about when they are out on the hustings. Let them find some real issue. There is no connection between this issue and the pipe line debate that took place ten years ago. That had to do with a matter of financing. This is a matter of sound economics for Canada, and I am glad of having the privilege to stand up and support it in this chamber.
Six o'clock.
Could we not have the usual courtesy extended to the house, this being Monday night, and adjourn until seven or 7.30 for a bite to eat?
Agreed.
In the interests of getting on with business I think we ought to go on sitting through.
You had better keep a quorum here.
The minister had better keep in mind what he has done if the government should ever decide to ask a courtesy, as asked for by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, when he wanted to adjourn.
If hon. members want one hour, I should have no objection to that.
I thought that the minister had refused. Would the minister reconsider adjourning for one hour?
Agreed.

If it is for one hour, I should be agreeable.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before we rose at six o'clock we had listened to a spirited defence of the government's approval of the arrangements for Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited to build a line south of the great lakes through the United States. That spirited defence was made by the hon. member for Bow River, and I think it would not be unfair to him to say that it was made mainly on the basis of dollars and cents.
I want to make it clear, Mr. Chairman, that we do not agree with the economic arguments advanced by the hon. member for Bow River, and other members of this group will deal with that phase of the matter. I propose to spend my time this evening on something that the hon. member for Bow River and others who take his position have overlooked, something that I feel is far more important than the dollars and cents or the economic aspect of this pipe line business. The something to which I refer as more important is the simple necessity of pledged words being kept.
I do not think that political life can enjoy the respect it ought to from the people of the country unless commitments that are solemnly made are kept. I intend by reference to the record, and as hon. members will see I have a number of books on my desk and a few more under it, to demonstrate that very firm commitments were given by Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited and the Liberal
[The Chairman.]
government of the day, when that company was incorporated and given its $80 million loan, that the company would not seek to put a line anywhere outside of Canada.
I am the first to admit that a company or a government, like an individual, has the right to change its mind. But if the company in question or the government of the day has changed its mind, surely the obligation of the government is to bring that change of mind before parliament for parliamentary approval. I insist that that is what must be done with respect to this permit to Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited or else we have got the 1956 situation all over again. We have got the government playing fast and loose with the rights of parliament.
First of all, Mr. Chairman, I would like to place on the record again, although this has been done on several occasions and interesting comments have been made about it, a key phrase in section 6(A) of chapter 92 of the Statutes of Canada for 1950-51. The title of the act is, "An Act to Incorporate Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited," and in section 6(a) it is clearly stated, as a proviso to the things that the company is allowed by its charter to do:
*-provided that the main pipe lines or lines, either for the transmission and transportation of gas or oil shall be located entirely within Canada-
[DOT] (7:10 p.m.)
I know there have been arguments already concerning whether or not there is an exception there which the company can exploit because of the reference to main line or lines. The Prime Minister of this country in his first statement, the one he issued on August 25, 1966, had no doubt about the meaning of this phrase because he said:
That act provides that the company may "within or outside Canada construct . . . pipe lines . . . provided that the main pipe line or lines . . . shall be located entirely within Canada". (Section 6(a)). While the line to be located outside Canada, to transfer gas from western to eastern Canada, would not be built by the company itself but by a partially owned subsidiary and while it might not at the outset be the main line, the government felt, as already stated, that it would almost inevitably become the main line and that the arrangement would not be in accord with the spirit of the policy laid down by parliament in the company's legislation.
I should like to take the members of the committee for a few minutes through what happened in 1951. I am now talking about a period five years prior to what we generally refer to as the pipe line debate of 1956. In the session of 1950-51 a Liberal private member,
October 31, 1966

Mr. Decore, the then member tor Vegreville, introduced Bill No. 75 to incorporate Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited. It was introduced after we had had several rather tumultuous experiences with earlier pipe line bills, several of which had not got through the house because they involved lines going out of this country. So Mr. Decore, when he introduced this bill, said very clearly as recorded at pages 734 and 735 of Hansard:
-I have been authorized to say that the very purpose of this proposed company is to build a gas pipe line from Alberta to Montreal, following an all-Canadian route, and paralleling the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway and of the Canadian National Railway. It will be approximately 2,200 miles long with collecting lines and lateral lines of 900 miles. In view of the type of debates we had on pipe line bills not so very long ago concerning an all-Canadian route I venture to say that some people got certain ideas and that may be the reason why this bill is before this house today.
Mr. Decore was perfectly right. It was in the context of the debate we had had in 1949 and 1950 that the company saw the light and came before parliament asking for incorporation only for the purpose of building an all-Canadian route. Later, at page 735, Mr. Decore, the then member for Vegreville, said:
There is of course another federal act which exercises control, namely, the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act.
By way of parenthesis I might say that that act has been repealed and replaced by the National Energy Board Act. He continued:
However, it is my opinion that this act would have no application, because all consumers will be in Canada and no gas will be exported out of Canada.
That was the clearly stated purpose of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited when it asked parliament to give it a charter, to do business in this country. The purpose was to build and operate an exclusively all-Canadian pipe line. As a result of the clear statement made to the house on February 27, 1951, by Mr. Decore, it is interesting to note the speeches that followed. The first member to speak for the Conservative party was Hon. Howard Green. The first member to speak for the C.C.F. of that day was the present member for Winnipeg North Centre. We both accepted Mr. Decore's assurance that the company was asking only for the right to build a pipe line in Canada and therefore we said there would not be a great delay in giving second reading to that bill. Since the debate occupied only about four pages in 23033-590i
Interim Supply
Hansard, this is clear confirmation that we kept to that promise.
The bill then went to the House of Commons standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I have before me the volume containing the reports of the sessions, of that committee dealing with this bill. I note with interest on page 10 of the proceedings for Tuesday, March 6, 1951, that a witness for the company, Mr. Frank August Schultz-he followed Mr. Tolmie who had spoken in rather general terms about the route of the line but made it clear it would be a line exclusively in Canada-testified as follows on that same day, as found on page 10 of the report:
The second consideration was that it should be an all-Canadian project, that it would be Canadian gas transported over an all-Canadian line, and that 100 per cent of the consumption would be in Canadian cities. It would be a project over which the Canadian government would have complete jurisdiction both as to the projected line and, ultimately, as far as the prices which are realized on the sale are concerned.
Would the hon. member give us the date of that?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I thought I gave it. It is March 6, 1951, in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. I was reading from page 10. During the sittings of this committee the next day, March 8, the members got down to clause 6(a), the one we are looking at today. In the original draft of the bill the phrase about the main line having to be in Canada was not there. The only thing in that clause which caused discussion was the opening phrase which read "within or outside Canada".
I invite hon. members, especially on the government side, to read from about page 68 to about page 78 of the report of the proceeds ings of that committee on March 8, 1951. The hon. member for Calgary North was on the committee. The hon. member for Kootenay West was on that committee and so were persons like Mr. Noseworthy, Mr. Herridge, Mr. Gillis and others who were members of the house at that time. You will discover that the members were concerned about the phrase "within or outside Canada". If I had the time I would read their exact words. They said in effect "you have given us the assurance it is an all-Canadian route you are going to build, but you have this little loophole in the words 'within or outside Canada'."

That was the story in 1951 and that is how Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited got its charter, by making this firm commitment. I want to say as I said at the outset that I am not going into the economics or the dollars and cents of this matter because my colleagues will do that, but even if it could be proven that it made better economic sense to do something other than was promised we must remember this little word "integrity" and this little matter of a commitment that was made in good faith. Parliament should not be played with in a fast and loose way in connection with this matter.
The year 1956 came along, and that is a year that those of us who were here and many people who were not here will never forget. There was presented to this house by the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe a bill which called upon parliament to approve an agreement under which $80 million was to be lent to this company to enable it to build the western section of an all-Canadian route. At the same time the government of Canada shared with the government of Ontario the cost of building a pipe line through northern Ontario so we could have an all-Canadian route. In 1956 sessional paper No. 174P was tabled; it contained a copy of the revised agreement which had been signed on May 8, 1956. I read many parts of that lengthy document into the record during the 1956 debate. Let me now read two or three things which appear on the opening page. There is a reference in the first paragraph to an allCanadian natural gas pipe line and another reference in the second paragraph. In the final paragraph on page 1 the following is stated:
And whereas it is in the public interest that the western section of the all-Canadian pipe line should be constructed in 1956 and the government of Canada should for this purpose make a temporary loan to Trans-Canada;
Now therefore this agreement witnesseth:-
The picture now begins to clear. The company was given a charter by the people through the parliament of Canada in 3951 on the clear understanding that it was going to build an all-Canadian pipe line and that it was to do business exclusively and entirely in Canada, but it was to have the right to go out of Canada to buy materials and to obtain money. Gas was to be transmitted in Canada to be sold in Canada and this was to be an all-Canadian route. When the company found it could not do this on its own it came to Mr. Howe and Mr. Howe agreed that public
Interim Supply
money would be lent to the company for the purpose of carrying out the stated intention of building an all-Canadian route.
We got into a debate about that in 1956. I have several of the volumes here. In reading through them over the week end. I was shocked again at what went on during the course of that debate. I do not intend to repeat all of it or relet the blood that was let in the course of that debate, but the same commitment was made again. Mr. Howe made a speech on the substance of the legislation on May 14, 1956. This was a speech on the resolution preceding the bill and he said at the end of it that he was giving notice of closure for the first time. That is the kind of debate we had. During the course of his speech he referred to it on about five occasions as an all-Canadian pipe line system. In looking at page 3860 I find that he said:
I am not going today to repeat the history of the all-Canadian pipe line project-
Later on, having given the views of various people, he said:
It was on this basis that the new company prepared its engineering and financing plans.
It was as clear as crystal in Mr. Howe's opening speech that a commitment was made in 1951 by the company and that we were being asked to lend this company the money to enable it to carry out the idea of an all-Canadian natural gas pipe line.
Later on when we got over other details of the debate-yes, it was on second reading-Mr. Howe returned to this matter and said, as recorded in Hansard for May 17, 1956, that this would be an all-Canadian company. These words are not hidden at all. You can pick up any of these volumes and find several places where a government member was speaking and insisting that there was a firm commitment that this would be an all-Canadian pipe line.
One of the themes used by Liberals in attacking the Tories during that debate as to other plans like the McMahon and Gairdner plans was that the virtue of the Liberal plan was that it was to be an all-Canadian project. At page 4025 of Hansard for May 17, 1956, Mr. Howe talked about proposals for other kinds of plans for sending gas from western Canada south into the United States and having gas come from the United States into eastern Canada. He said that the government had rejected these proposals because it felt that gas should be brought to eastern Canada

October 31. 1966
Interim Supply
by an all-Canadian pipe line. Mr. Howe is reported as having said:
That position was rather resented in Alberta. The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Nickle) has spoken about it in the House of Commons. It is claimed that we are putting an improper tax on the owners of the gas and making the project of supplying that gas to Canadians in eastern Canada uneconomical.
1 want to read the next paragraph which is about 20 lines to show what was being said by this Canadian whose voice is being sent to us from across the years. He said:
I went to Calgary at the invitation of the petroleum institute and addressed its members there at a dinner meeting. I was warned beforehand that I must submit myself to questioning after the meeting was over. I went there for the purpose of explaining why it is in the national interest that eastern Canada be served with Alberta natural gas through an all-Canadian pipe line. I had the honour of having my friend, the hon. member for Calgary South, sit beside me on that occasion.
[DOT] (7:30 p.m.)
Whether I was able to convice him that evening, or whether he has seen the light since, I am not sure. But I think perhaps at some stage we have made progress in a meeting of minds on the proper method for distributing western Canadian gas. I explained the need for an all-Canadian line.
Mr. Chairman, one could almost think that these experts were put in there for the benefit of strengthening my arguments. I am just quoting Mr. Howe speaking his own mind on this issue. He then went on to say:
I admitted that it would be more costly than alternative plans, but I said the added cost is one of the penalties we must accept for Canadian nationhood. I remember my words. I said: "There is a price on Canadian nationhood. If we always looked for the cheapest way of doing things here in Canada there might have been another state in the United States but there very likely would have been no Canada. From confederation the people of Canada have been very jealous about accepting any monetary advantage that would in any way jeopardize the control by Canada over her own resources."
I see my time is running out Mr. Chairman, but perhaps I might come back to this subject later in the debate. But I must refer to the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner's speech, the whole theme of which was that the Tories were going to sell out to the Americans and that it was the Liberals who by this all-Canadian line, this 100 per cent Canadian line, were doing a service to this country. Their quarrel *with us in that day was only that we wanted it publicly owned.
I have mentioned Mr. Howe and I have mentioned Mr. Gardiner. The prime minister of the day, Mr. St. Laurent, did not have a

great deal to say on the substance of the bill. He got mixed up in the debate on closure, which I am sure he must regret, but even he made the situation clear on May 22, 1956, and I quote from page 4173 of Hansard:
As to the first point, I agree completely with the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat. All of us want this to be an all-Canadian pipe line, to be a pipe line controlled under Canadian law and to be operated for the benefit of the development of Canada at large.
I can pick up quotations of Mr. Garson, who was then minister of justice, of Mr. Lesage, then minister of northern affairs and national resources, and demonstrate how one by one they all said the same thing, that this was to be an all-Canadian route. The commitment had been made crystal clear by Trans-Canada in 1951. It continued to the commitment of this government. Those of us who were here at that time I am sure will never forget the last speech made by Mr. Howe in that debate. It was on June 1 and it appears at page 4631 of Hansard. We were experiencing closure at that time. The house was full and so were the galleries. Mr. Howe made the statement that he thought this would probably be his last project for Canada. He emphasized that this allCanadian pipe line was being built for Canada and that no matter how much fighting there might be over the bill, his children would be glad that their dad had a part in building it. I am not trying to be emotional in bringing in C. D. Howe; I would be the last one to do that.

speechtext:
May I add just one more sentence? I have much more to say but I will have to say it later. I wish to say, in conclusion of this chapter in my speech, that there is no denying the right of the government to change its position and there is no denying the right of the company to come back to parliament and ask for its act of incorporation to be changed. But if parliament is not asked to make such changes the government and the company have no right to act in bad faith and try to circumvent the legislation. They have no right to do what it was clearly promised would not be done. I call for a clear explanation. I call on the government to bring this matter back before parliament and I hope it will do so before I have to get into the debate again with further interesting quotations showing very clearly the position that was taken by the government of that day.
October 31, 1966

Mr. Chairman, like the previous speaker I will have to make my remarks chapter by chapter. Before doing so, however, I wish to take a line from the previous speaker who referred to closure at another time in this house. The thought occurred to me then that perhaps the exercise we are going through in the matter of defence is in many ways not unlike that closure debate. We have entered upon this interim supply debate in a very trying atmosphere, particularly from the point of view of the question of defence. Very difficult and extremely arduous conditions have been set down by the Minister of National Defence. Indeed, these were clearly portrayed as recently as October 18 when the minister together with the chief of defence staff, General Allard, Air Marshal Sharpe, vicechief, Vice-Admiral Hennessy, comptroller general, Air Marshal Reyno, chief of personnel, Lieut. General Lilley, chief of technical services; Commodore Murdoch, chief of plans and Major General Dare, deputy chief of reserves met in Toronto at a private dinner meeting with representatives of the Trio organization in Canada. I bring this in, Mr. Chairman, just to illustrate the difficulties under which we are attempting, on behalf of those who are interested, and there are many many thousands of them in Canada, indeed, everybody who pays taxes-
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman-
I have the floor, Mr. Chairman. Does the minister wish to ask a question?
Yes. Would my hon. friend tell me where he got the information that this meeting was in Toronto? Did he get it from his military adviser, Admiral Brock, or did he get it from another source?

My source was the horse's mouth. At this meeting in Toronto attended by five senior members of the Tri-Service Identity Organization, those very responsible men, some of them quite recently in the Canadian armed services, were left with one impression. They were left with the clear impression that everything possible would be done by the minister and his staff to ensure that no one who is critical in any way of his plans for unification and integration will be permitted the opportunity of appearing before the House of Commons defence committee when and if the minister ever gets around to calling it.
Interim Supply
[DOT] (7:40 p.m.)
This, Mr. Chairman, is the atmosphere in which we must try to work and in which we appeal to the minister. But his mind is made up. He closed the door some months ago-indeed, he slammed it-on the House of Commons when he tampered, as it has been called, with the evidence of Rear Amiral Landymore.
In this connection most of the record has now come to light. The persistence of the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona and others has brought the minister to the position where he has seen fit to produce and table the two versions, the one which the Admiral and his Maritime Command staff has prepared for the benefit of members of parliament and the one that he was permitted to present after what a usually reliable source in the minister's office described as something from the mouth usually referred to in children as diarrhoea got through with it.
This is but part of the story. We will not have all of it until we are given the opportunity of hearing the Admiral before the defence committee, which is the proper place. Part of the testimony which has been referred to and discussed widely in the press and on the floor of this house still remains to be put on the record, and I intend to read it now.
I have before me what is described as a statutory declaration made by Rear Admiral Landymore in order to meet some of the allegations and charges that have been made in regard to his appearance before the defence committee. He has stated as follows:
I,	William M. Landymore, of West Lawrencetown, in the county of Halifax, province of Nova Scotia, do solemnly declare.
1.	That I have personal knowledge of the matters herein contained and declared to.
2.	I was requested by the standing committee on defence to appear before them on the 23rd of June, 1966 to provide a briefing on Maritime Command. I prepared for the committee the information I believed necessary to give them a clear understanding of the state of the command.
3.	I prepared two briefs for the standing committee. First, an unclassified brief which could be fully reported in the minutes, and second, a classified brief on operations which could not be reported.
4.	I delivered both briefs orally to the Minister of National Defence on the 22nd of June, at his request, in the form and detail intended for the standing committee on defence.
5.	I was, through my attending staff officers, required to hand over to the minister's staff a copy of the unclassified brief, that is, the brief which would be reported in the minutes.

forces and in civilian occupations supporting the armed services. In addition, we have 1,200 people who are directly employed in aircraft parts manufacture, aircraft overhaul and repair. That industry, incidentally, is almost totally dependent on defence production and purchasing. Also, more than 1,000 people now work on the repair and overhaul of ships and ship components. Five hundred more people work in the more delicate and sophisticated communications equipment field. Another 200 to 300 people are employed in the production of sonar equipment which is of such high calibre that it gives Canada one of the most efficient underwater detection forces in the world today. The minister has said this often and I agree with him. The only thing wrong is that the ships are not at sea. They are tied to the docks.
You are at sea.
The minister and I appear to be the only ones at sea. There are no ships there.
Speak for yourself.
