This is also confirmed by the failure of the Minister of National Defence to contradict this statement clearly in order to set the record straight with regard to what the chief of defence staff said. That failure must also be taken as confirmation of the intended role
Interim Supply
for the R.C.N. That is one side of the confirmation. The other side of the confirmation lies in the failure of the minister to let the defence committee meet for any purpose prior to the introduction of the legislation which will deal the final blow to our defence services. Why he should want to carry out this major step in the manner that he has remains beyond all comprehension. These are things that all servicemen are wondering about. Many of the backbenchers on the minister's side are also wondering about them. I am sure that if the minister bothered advising his colleagues in cabinet they would also wonder why things are being done as they are.
It has been suggested that perhaps the minister is trying to hide something. I agree with that. I think he is trying to hide something. He is trying to hide his own confused state of mind about the tiger he has by the tail, because he does not know what to do with it.
That is right.

We shall question the
Minister of National Defence during the course of the next few days about his premises with regard to unification and integration, his premises that they would save the country money, that they would provide for greater and more efficient services. We have evidence other than newspaper articles and other matter which has come before us during the last three or four months to indicate that the minister's premises are wrong.
We will show graphically and pictorially that the matters to be dealt with are much more serious than they would appear to the minister at his level in this game of do away with the services. We shall show that integration so far has produced such little gems as bringing the cost of a 45 cent engine block drain up to $451 and some cents. I am not sure about the cents. We will show, for example, and this fact is demonstrable, that the amount of paper going into his integrated command headquarters for purposes of administration has gone up so fantastically that the increase itself can be measured in terms of tonnage. I have not got around to counting the pencils yet but I shall.
The whole question of the integration and unification of the Canadian armed forces is one that should not be dealt with until the people of Canada have had an opportunity to understand fully the implications of what the

October 31. 1966
Interim Supply
minister intends to do. We should not be satisfied, now or ever, with the impression that everything will be done to prevent anybody who is critical of this plan voicing his concern. As the junior member for Halifax I do not intend to let that happen. There are about 1,100 or 1,200 questions which need serious consideration and answers by the minister before he can with honour bring this house a measure designed to disrupt and abolish not only our current defence structure and the traditional pattern of defence but all those men who have spent the greater part of their lives working toward meaningful defence postures for Canada in the eyes of the world.
[DOT] (8:00 p.m.)
If the minister has any feeling or concern for Canada he must spell out to the people and to the House of Commons just how it is he intends to save money. It is not enough to say that cut-backs up to 60 per cent can be achieved in some cases. That is not the answer. It does not show us where the dollars and cents are being saved. Do not tell us you can save 60 per cent in administration costs at the dockyards in Halifax without telling us where it will pop up elsewhere in the administrative structure.
Let the minister tell us the full story. Let him not hide under the guise of acting in the best interests of the country. Let him not try to tell the people that we have the best and most efficient underwater defence structure in the world. At least, let him not tell me that. I see it every weekend when I am home-tied up to the docks. What good is it if it is tied up there? Why have men left the navy? Why do hundreds and hundreds of them write to me? Surely the minister is not fooling anybody when he says blandly in the press that his visit to Halifax was a most interesting and informative one. Surely he does not pretend to be fooling anybody. Why does he say these things? We know he was booed and heckled. He had no right to put officers and men of the armed services in a position where they felt impelled to react. How could Canada contemplate a position where an admiral in the navy would have to tell his men to sit down and shut up? What kind of a country do we live in when we permit such things to be done to the infrastructure that men's emotions are driven to a loss of concern for dignity and a loss of respect for authority?

These are things which have happened. It is useless for the minister to deny it. Surely he must have seen from what took place that somewhere along the line he was possibly not 100 per cent right and that somebody else might possibly have a view which ought to be considered.
I am one of these-the minister is not aware of this but it is not my fault-who would be quite prepared to sit down in the defence committee and listen to answers, answers which are not facetious or tongue-incheek or emanating from some sycophant in the minister's office. Let him talk to us and tell us what he wants to do. Does he wish to abandon present defence policies? If he wants to change them, maybe he is right. But until he tells us what it is he wants to do, he must not expect us to support him.
We have wasted a good deal of time over this business, time which might perhaps have been better devoted to other matters. All the minister had to do to take this matter out of the House of Commons was to say: by all means let the defence committee sit, if there is a feeling that it did not have full opportunity to question the witnesses brought before it.
I have not heard any member of the defence committee complain about the meetings being a waste of time. The minister is the only one who has made that complaint. I am prepared to sit at seven o'clock in the morning or at midnight if there is any question of interfering with the time of the house. Let us talk with people other than the minister who can tell us meaningful things about the direction in which present defence policy is carrying us and where it is to end. If the minister wishes to have a highly mobile police force to place at the disposal of the United Nations to help them clean up their problems around the world, then let us talk about that. But let us not follow the invidious practice of encouraging people to say one thing privately and another publicly. Let us bring some sense and reason to these considerations and take a first step by letting the defence committee look again at the evidence.
Had the witnesses who appeared before that committee during the winter months not been reluctant to talk freely, perhaps this debate on interim supply would not have been necessary. This is not the best place in which to go into details of what is happening in terms of dollars and cents or to discuss the impact upon regional economies of any serious tampering with the present structure. It

should be done in committee. It should be done in a manner which would give the areas affected ample opportunity to prepare themselves. The business community in Halifax should have something more positive to go on than the disguised approach which the minister has adopted up to this point.

Mr. Chairman, one of the unfortunate things about debates on interim supply is the fact that they bounce around from subject to subject. I regret very much it was not possible for me to be in the chamber earlier today when the subject I want to speak on, Great Lakes Transmission and Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, was first brought up but, like my colleague the hon. member for Port Arthur, unfortunately I had a very important committee meeting to attend and it was with a certain amount of surprise I came back into the chamber and found that this subject was being discussed. Therefore possibly hon. members will excuse me if my remarks are not as rounded and as fully researched as I would have preferred them to be.
This is a subject of very great importance to northwestern Ontario and I find myself in the classic position, along with Edmund Burke, of trying to decide what is the responsibility of a member to the nation, whether I should stand four-square for my region against the interests of the nation or for the interests of the nation against the interests of my region.
23033-591 i
Interim Supply
My region is a natural resource producing area and, generally speaking, every such area I have visited suffers from the same disability. Such a region is continually exploited by centres outside its control. It has a very limited amount of control over its own existence and it always seems to be subject to the forces which come into it from without.
In my area there is a sense of frustration, a feeling that we do not have command over our own resources. Even more important is the feeling that forces work against us to make sure that we do not get the services we require from the provincial government, while the federal government seems to step, over us to move from Toronto to Winnipeg,! with no stops in between to deal with our very pressing problem.
To give you an example, Mr. Chairman, it has come to my knowledge today that a distillery company has been looking over the Canadian lakehead as a possible place to build a new plant. I am told that the men involved like it. They know it has an adequate labour supply, adequate industrial land and adequate supplies of fuel. But they are not going to locate there. They are going to locate on Georgian Bay, not because condi-i tions are any better there but because Georgian Bay happens to be in a portion of the country which comes under the government's area development program. It is this sort of apparent discrimination which makes the people of my area very fed up and frustrated with governments at various levels.
With this background out of the way I would now like to say a few words about the proposal which Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited has submitted and which the federal government has accepted. It concerns the building of the Great Lakes Transmission pipe line from Emerson, Manitoba, through to Sarnia, Ontario, and the so called by-passing of northern Ontario for a period of ten years.
I think it is fairly evident that there are two main issues involved, first, the emotional issue and second, the question of gas. I think I have given some of the background to the emotional issue. We feel that our interests are not being fully considered because the northern line through northern and northwestern Ontario is not being looped or twinned. We feel we are losing certain economic advantages as a result of this in the form of municipal taxes, in the form of jobs as construction goes through and in the form of continuing maintenance. These are simple facts, and for the present we will lose these

October 31. 1966
Interim Supply
things. The pipe line itself is a symbol of our belonging to the country, of belonging to Canada, and we are not going to have that feeling of belonging.
Then, we get into the more difficult area which concerns the question of gas. On two or three occasions I have read exhaustively the National Energy Board report to the Governor in Council concerning the application of Trans-Canada Pipe Lines Limited and in spite of myself, in spite of my regional emotions, I find that we are not getting as bad a deal as we anticipated.
On August 25,	1966, when the Prime
Minister in a press release announced that the government had turned down Trans-Canada's original proposal, I was one of those who were very happy, very pleased indeed, as were all my constituents. But we were all shocked and surprised when, according to the press release issued on October 4, the decision that the Governor in Council had reached on August 25 was apparently reversed.
The reason for this apparent reversal was the fact that in the August 25 press release the Prime Minister said nothing about the continuation of negotiations between the National Energy Board and Trans-Canada, and so we were led to believe by that press release and the manner in which it was reported that it was only a matter of time until Trans-Canada went ahead and built a twin line through northern Ontario.
In spite of the fact that the second press release did answer all the objections which I personally had, objections which I raised with the ministers concerned, I was still shocked at the news because we had not been prepared for it. It seems to me that one of the government's great faults, and a fault of ordinary members too, is that we have not mastered the use of the media which enable us to communicate with our constituents, with the result that when we do make changes and shift our positions, the public does not have the background knowledge which is so necessary if it is to understand what is taking place.
I come now to the question of gas or, to put it another way, industrial development for northwestern Ontario. This to me is of supreme importance because of the fact that with gas we have an opportunity to broaden our industrial base. During the course of debate on this subject some rather uninformed and on occasion ridiculous statements

have been made. One is recorded at page 9227 of Hansard for October 28:
The line which is now being approved by the government will be the main line, and the requirement that Trans-Canada will twin its northern line, commencing in 1970, means that for 15 years this government has placed a moratorium upon industrial and economic expansion in northern Ontario.
These words were spoken by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and, Mr. Chairman, if you will allow me to say so, they show a complete lack of knowledge of the situation as it exists.
One of the reasons for this agreement, in fact one of the advantages that will accrue to us, is that we will be getting lower priced gas as a result of the agreement, plus the fact that we are to have increased supplies of gas made available to us. In other words, while we have to get over the emotional aspect of not getting the pipe line, we must remember that we will be getting additional supplies of gas at a cheaper price. This is a point which was exhaustively gone into by the National Energy Board several times.
This is based upon the fact that by lowering the price to the people to whom it supplies gas Trans-Canada expects to find a larger market for its product. By looping a line through the United States and bringing the western supplies of gas to eastern and southwestern Ontario it anticipates that the capacity of the northern line, which passes through northern Ontario, will be made available to northern Ontario for its industrial and economic expansion. So while we may not be getting all we want, and one never does, we will be getting increased supplies of gas and we will be getting that gas at a less expensive price.
As a matter of fact, to give one example, Northern and Central Gas Company, on the basis of the Great Lakes project, has contracted with two of the mines in my constituency, Steep Rock Mines and Caland Ore to provide them with gas at cheaper prices. The actual difference is 3.4 cents per m.c.f. on the basis of the Great Lakes Transmission project going through. But if this project does not go through then it would seem reasonable to me to anticipate that the price to these companies would go up, which would have the effect of putting a damper on our economic expansion.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

Certainly.

Does the hon. member have any idea what the price of gas might be if the northern line were twinned now?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, If you will take a look at the National Energy Board report, page 5-2, you will find a chapter entitled "Canadian Markets-Evidence." I read from page 5-2:
-Trans-Canada indicated that the total demand in Canada during the 10 years to 1976 would be some 11 per cent below the level estimated "with Great Lakes".
The reason for that is that they would not be able to sell the volume to bring about a cut in price on the basis of increased volume. The last sentence in the paragraph reads:
The rates that might be available to distributors should the Great Lakes project not be built were not specified, but Trans-Canada suggested that its current rates or higher ones were indicated.
In other words, we would not get any decrease in the price of the fuel which we desperately need if we are to expand. This project seems to me to be a very good thing for our area which is in desperate need of this type of assistance from government. It is interesting to see that this type of assitance is not coming from government; it is coming from a private company. To back up that last statement further, because I wish to be thorough, on page 5-3 there is a table giving for the years 1967-76 the estimates of market potential for natural gas in all of Canada. This is outlined with the Great Lakes project and without the Great Lakes project, which I interpret to mean the twinning of the lines through northern Canada. For my area and all of northwestern and northern Ontario the difference in volume per cent will be directly attributable to our increased volume of gas. This will be 9.6 per cent and on this we are to get, as I said, a reduction of 3.4 cents per m.c.f. Therefore we are not getting too bad a deal at all.
On behalf of those from northern Ontario and northwestern Ontario who presented their case before the National Energy Board and those who organized a delegation from northwestern Ontario to press this point upon the government, I think at this time I should indicate their thanks to the members of parliament from northwestern Ontario and to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the Minister of Energy, Mines, and Resources for
Interim Supply
taking time off during a very crucial dominion-provincial tax conference to meet our delegation and discuss and explain these things. This is a courtesy and we recognize it as such; we are appreciative of it.
The other thing I should like to talk about is what guarantee are we going to have that we are going to get a twinning of the northern pipe line, because it has been well pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that there has been a certain commitment by Trans-Canada that the main pipe line must be in Canada. I think all of us realize that our party will support that position. What guarantees do we have? There are a variety spelled out in the document which the Minister of Energy, Mines, and Resources tabled yesterday.
Trans-Canada has covenanted with the government of Canada to begin building another pipe line through northern and northwestern Ontario in 1970. There are two points to this. First and most important is the fact that the pipe line must remain Canadian. Second, Trans-Canada has given assurance to the government that 60 per cent of the volume of natural gas transported each year by Trans-Canada from western to eastern Canada will be transported through the northern Ontario line. To accomplish this, in the light of its growing markets Trans-Canada will begin on its own initiative to twin the northern line.
It is further provided in this agreement that after the fine is completed they must provide a minimum of 65 per cent of Canadian requirements through the northern line. The obvious assumption from this is that the line going through the United States will become mainly an export line presumably to pay for the construction of the northern line. In item 5 on page 9 of the document Trans-Canada, if it does not fulfil its obligations and if it is not prevented from doing so by an act of God such as a hydrogen bomb explosion, binds itself to pay $1 million to the government. This is a rather substantial amount. I do not think this agreement was entered into in a light way.
The third point is, what will happen to Great Lakes? Is there any guarantee that Trans-Canada will not sell it for a quick capital gain? The answer to that is in clause 8 on page 10 of the agreement, whereby 50 per cent of the shares which are to accrue to Trans-Canada are to be deposited in trust with the government. Therefore the company

October 31. 1966
Interim Supply
will not, without the consent of the government of Canada, dispose of its 50 per cent of the interest in Great Lakes Transmission.
As I said before it is most unfortunate I was not able to be here when this topic was brought up, but I did hear part of the speech made by the hon. member for Bow River and the speech made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. Needless to say I disagree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on grounds of philosophy. I do not believe that we as a country or that northwestern Ontario as a section of Canada should be inward-looking. I believe we should look outward because the world is a big place and we have a large role to play if we can find the courage of our convictions.
We in northwestern Ontario feel that in many ways we have been hurt by the arrangement the government has entered into all times. I think this is absolutely true. In the future, when governments make arrangements which affect the welfare of any region I believe they have an obligation to get into contact with the people of the region and explain precisely what they are trying to do. The type of performance we have had from the government in this pipe line issue is typical of something which has to be eradicated. It is necessary to take people into one's confidence, and in this case the government did not. Perhaps it is because for the first time in a long while northwestern Ontario has not had a representative in the cabinet that our interests are not fully looked after. There are, as I am sure hon. members of the official opposition sitting on the back benches know, very stringent limitations on back bench members when conclusions already have been reached.
I should like to think that the ambition of the people in northwestern Ontario is to look forward to the time when they can settle their own fate and do not have to come to the government hat in hand. We resent the attitude of the government in this matter. We recognize there are certain benefits for us in it and we accept them gladly. We look forward to the building of the second line through northern Ontario in 1970-or else.

Mr. Chairman, I congratulate the last speaker on the extent to which he seems to have defended the government on the basis of saying, as they have so often done: We have now made up our minds,

please, oh please, do not confuse us with the facts. That seems to be the policy of the Minister of National Defence and if the committee will bear with me I propose to discuss the untenable position into which the government has got itself as a result of what I can only, in considered terms, describe as an improper, unconstitutional and illegal position taken by the minister with regard to committee hearings and the methods and means by which witnesses are to be examined.
This subject has been touched on in part by the hon. member for Calgary North. The hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona dealt with this matter quite specifically, but I propose to refer to this aspect only collaterally. I do not suggest that it is transcendent in importance to the main points they have brought forward. Nothing can transcend the gravity and importance of problems of national defence.
I suggest that the position in which the government has now placed itself as a result of statements made by the minister and confirmed by the Prime Minister must give us pause for thought. The hon. member for Calgary North earlier today put on record statements that have not been denied by the Minister of National Defence which were contained in a news report and subsequently repeated by him outside this house. I think that quite obviously these are his definite views.
It is strange that what in a minister is decisive, strong and bold often becomes stubborn, dogmatic and bull-headed. This position has been reinforced by the Prime Minister. I asked the Prime Minister on October 17 if he subscribed to the view expressed by the Minister of National Defence that serving officers can only give evidence to committees when allowed to do so by the minister and that their evidence must conform to the views of the minister irrespective of the facts. I then called it to the attention of the minister and the government that if this were carried to its extreme it would not be in keeping with the Senate and House of Commons Act, section 249, which says that the Senate and the House of Commons may administer the oath to witnesses examined at the bar of the said houses. By practice the rules which prevail with regard to the Senate and the house have been carried into the committee structure.
The minister has now taken a position which I suggest is unconstitutional; yet he feels this position is all right. Let me place on
October 31, 1966

record the fact that with a great flourish of trumpets the government said in the last parliament that it was producing changes in the rules, including a new committee structure which would be a great benefit and which this house must have. This was the statement made during the debate, as found on page 12544 of Hansard for March 18, 1965:
As far as committees are concerned, and the work of committees-and this is the main subject of this report-there is no doubt that we do not use the committees system to its best advantage.
The next sentence contains a reference to myself and with due modesty I will omit it. The Prime Minister is then reported as having said:
This is a situation which has occupied the attention of all students of democratic parliamentary institutions in recent years, because with the executive you have not only the cabinet but you have behind the cabinet a growing body of expert officialdom which is inevitably becoming more and more important as government becomes increasingly complex.
I remember some years ago attending a luncheon in London, England, of some senior officials of the British government, departmental heads and some cabinet ministers. One of the ministers said to me as we sat down: "Here is the government of the United Kingdom, with two or three ministers." There is this problem-the growth of the executive, the new despotism, as Lord Hewart called it, and how to prevent it destroying the efficiency of the legislature. Could we strengthen the legislature by deepening and broadening the committees structure? There are some recommendations in this report which, I believe, when implemented may well have this effect.
Let me emphasize these final words:
-but after the committee had been set up it was surely not only the responsibility but the obligation of the government to leave it to do its work.
That was what the Prime Minister said on March 18, 1965. Those were his views at that time.
Let me refer to what the Minister without Portfolio has said, though I am not sure whether he had acquired his present eminence at that time. On March 19, 1965, as reported at page 12587 of Hansard, the Minister without Portfolio said:
-it is our duty here, as representatives of a working democracy, to restore the balance between freedom and efficiency-
Later he said, and this is a very correct statement:
This reform would achieve two main results. First, it would allow an individual member of parliament access to information upon which to base intelligent criticism.

How in the name of heaven can a member make an intelligent criticism if he is not allowed in committee meetings to ask witnesses factual questions and receive factual answers? Are witnesses to be compelled to prepare their evidence to meet the views of their ministers? If that is so we might just as well throw our whole committee structure out the window.
The Minister without Portfolio said, having regard to the average member:
As a result of his power on that committee he will be able to call witnesses either from the civil service or from outside government to give him the information and the documentation on the basis of which he can make decisions. Evidence from civil servants and other summoned before the committee to testify as to the facts concerning the proposed legislation will make each member of the committee a more intelligent critic.
Let me relate that to the public accounts committee of which I have some knowledge. How in the world would it be possible for the public accounts committee, the function of which is to inquire into complaints which the Auditor General has made about certain things he has found in the course of his examination, to perform its task efficiently? How could it be possible for the members of this committee to honestly, intelligently and conscientiously discharge their responsibilities without being free to call civil servants, including deputy ministers?
It is my suggestion that since time immemorial committees have been free to call witnesses to give evidence as to facts, irrespective of what a minister may want to be given as evidence by those witnesses. That is the problem we are facing today. What will be the thoughts of civil servants and serving officers who read Hansard and examine the statement made by the Minister of National Defence as to his view about the function of witnesses? What will be the thoughts of those civil servants who may be called in future to give evidence? Are they going to think as a result of the statement made by the minister and confirmed by the Prime Minister that they will have to check with their minister before giving evidence? If they are called, are we to take it that they must go to the minister and say: "Sir, here is what we intend to say. What would you suggest we should delete? What is your policy?"
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
This is somewhat similar to what happened during the course of the war. I do not remember the exact details but I think we

October 31, 1966
Interim Supply
were told that if we were taken prisoner all we had to give was our rank, name and serial number. Other hon. members can tell me if I am wrong. This is exactly what civil servants will be-name, rank and number witnesses. A deputy minister will say: "I am the deputy minister; I have seen my minister. He is a good minister and I like his policy." This is as far as they will go. It may be a question of reductio ad absurdum but I do not think it is.
I have said before in the house and elsewhere that governments must increasingly accept greater responsibilities as they face more complex and difficult tasks. They are facing great industrial complexes and great trade unions so they must be free to move rapidly and with greater flexibility. Every statute that we see contains somewhere within it the right to make ministerial decisions, the right to move by order in council, the right to act by regulation.
Recently we were discussing the question of the importation of Volkswagens. This is an illustration of what takes place day after day in the business of the government. At times I am prepared to accede to the requests of the government and give them the power they seek but on condition that we have the opportunity to call before us, through the committee structure for which I give credit to the government, witnesses for the purpose of examining and questioning the extent to which the government has used the powers we have given it. We want to examine whether they are operating well and functioning properly and the extent to which we can improve on those functions. If we do not have that opportunity then I think we will have to start saying no to the government when it asks for increased powers.
Let us take the particular instance of Admiral Landymore's evidence. I have read with some care the transcript of what Admiral Landymore intended to say and what he did say. I doubt that a witness should either be asked or compelled to answer questions on direct government policy.
I think the chairman of the committee has the right and duty to stop such a question or answer, and the witness himself has the right to say that this is an infringement on the domain of the government. However, there should be absolutely no restriction on anything else the witness may want to say. What is it that Admiral Landymore said? I refer members of the committee to pages 18, 22, 23, 24 and 25 of the brief. I will not go into all these statements but on pages 23 and 24 alone

there are two very brief statements which I will repeat to the committee to illustrate my point. On page 23 there is this statement which Admiral Landymore had included in his brief:
However, there has been a significant decline in re-engagements tor the subsequent terms. Over the same period of three years there has been a 10 per cent decrease in men re-engaging for their final term, and a 6 per cent decrease in those re-engaging for the third time. This represents a serious loss of our most valuable senior men.
How can this be anything else than a statement which it not only is the right of the admiral to give but his duty to give, and any attempt to suppress it is an infringement on his freedom.

As I was saying, the minister and the associate minister or one of their civilian officials, usually the deputy minister, have spoken for the Department of National Defence, and serving officers of the armed forces have merely been consulted in respect of technical questions. In addition, discussion of national defence estimates was usually limited to the consideration of supply in committee of the whole house and on those occasions when special committees on defence were set up or matters pertaining to defence were considered by the public accounts committee examination was almost always limited to past events and not a discussion of current expenditure or future defence policy.
Two new peacetime precedents have therefore been set by this government: first, the establishment of a standing committee on defence to consider current and future defence policy. This is a complete departure from previous practice and in fact you will find many pages of Hansard full of eloquent argument as to why special or standing committees on defence should not be constituted to consider defence policy.
You took the opposite view.

My hon. friend is quite right. The Prime Minister and I felt, however, on the basis of our experience in opposition, that the lack of such a committee meant that inadequate information on defence matters was available to members of parliament and, through their deliberations, to the Canadian people. We felt that the quality of debate would be improved and that the background information required for intelligent discussion of defence matters warranted the establishment of a defence committee notwithstanding the historical objections. Consequently, Mr. Chairman, the committee has been established, and I think on balance it has been most useful and has in fact filled the function of providing opportunity for a more thorough

examination not just of defence expenditures but of the policies associated with those expenditures.
The second departure has been the appearance of senior military commanders to make statements and answer questions. It is a matter for debate whether this is in fact desirable under the parliamentary system. With a full appreciation of the obvious risks involved I felt it would be worth while to see if some practical midway point could be reached between the United States congressional and the traditional parliamentary systems which would enable members of parliament to get a better appreciation of military matters directly from the people involved. I have therefore concurred from time to time in the appearance of military officers to make statements and to give testimony. I felt that this departure from custom was in order at this time when we are undertaking such a fundamental reorganization and when there are so many complex technical questions that could best be answered by the military staff themselves.
This does not mean and cannot mean, of course, that departmental officials and serving officers appear before the parliamentary committee as private individuals speaking on their own behalf. They are there as representatives of the department.
I should like to quote from the editorial page of tonight's Ottawa Citizen an article by Ben Malkin:
The constitutional position is clear enough. A departmental official should not criticize departmental policy in public, either explicitly or implicitly. The minister answers for policy, and the minister alone. And the minister takes the responsibility for policy. If it were otherwise, the cabinet, although established to make policy, would lose control to its departmental officials; this would be intolerable in a parliamentary democracy.
I should now like to refer to the book "Cabinet Government" by Sir Ivor Jennings. At page 118 he states:
The real reason for having ministers at the head of departments is, however, that this is an effective method of bringing government under public control.
Later on he states:
Under our constitution it is impossible to place any direct control over the army, over army organization, in the hands of any man except one who shall be directly responsible to the House of Commons.

In his book "Government of Canada" Robert MacGregor Dawson describes ministerial responsibility at page 219 of his book as follows:
The minister can never afford to forget that he will be expected to defend and justify his department's policies before parliament and the country. And yet at the same time he realizes that his policies must be technically and administratively sound if they are to meet the need which has called them into being. Inasmuch as the minister is politically responsible for everything done in his department, he is given supreme authority and he therefore has the power to overrule any of his civil servants at any time.
Even in the United States congressional system it is clear that the elected officials have not only the right but the duty to see that their policies are fairly presented to the people. In Theodore Sorensen's book entitled "Kennedy", in the section on speech and statement clearances, you will find the following:
The President reviewed some speeches on his own. Occasionally he would ask us to co-ordinate in advance and monitor in progress all congressional testimony by administration witnesses with differing points of view on a sensitive issue under hearing...
Some important gains resulted. Several defence department speeches were rendered less, "missile-rattling" ... The speeches most difficult to check- and most dangerous to leave unchecked-were those by high ranking military officers, whose remarks had not always reflected the President's point of view about peace... But it was clearer than ever that military officers on active duty were not to undermine the final decisions of their commander in chief in their speeches or legislative testimony, not to confuse the world about the nature of America's foreign policy, and not to undertake as an official responsibility the political indoctrination of either their troops or public opinion.
While in Canada the Governor General is commander in chief on behalf of Her Majesty, the minister and the government responsible to the House of Commons have the duty to see that their policies and programs are fairly presented. It is fundamental to our parliamentary practice that the minister responsible for a department will have the sole discretion as to the limits of the special material that his officers may present.

I don't know what you are talking about and you don't know either. I know I have been talking to Admiral Brock and to other people trying to get information, to get facts which this minister has been trying desperately to hide.
Do you deny such a document exists, that there was in fact a memo prepared by Admiral Brock?
I have no idea of such a document.
You have no idea? Are you denying there was such a document?

I am not responsible for Admiral Brock's actions and testimony. I am sure he has given the minister briefs but I don't know whether the minister has destroyed them. Admiral Brock told me he has given the Prime Minister a brief but I don't know whether the Prime Minister has destroyed it. I am not responsible for his actions, just for my own.
This raises a very important point of principle and it should be explored-
On a question of privilege-

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, the Minister of National Defence is very concerned about the authenticity of a document and he has made some suggestions. My hand lies very deeply in that document and I am very concerned with it. The minister talked about drafts that were

changed, and one thing and another. The first
19	were destroyed; indeed, the first 19 were burned. What came out of it I hope will be presented publicly at the right time to the Canadian people and will represent a viable, reasonable and worthy alternative to the utter nonsense we have listened to over the last
20	minutes. It is a very valid document.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, I must say that my hon. friend has gone up a lot in my esteem-
Hear, hear.
On a point of order, the minister was granted an extension of time for five minutes and no more. If no one else wishes to speak, I should like to have the floor.

On the point of order raised, we are in committee and I distinctly heard the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona make a speech. So if you recognize the minister now, Mr. Chairman, he has the right to another 30 minutes.

Mr. Chairman, I am quite willing to yield the floor to my hon. friend from Winnipeg South Centre. I will be speaking again later in the debate, if further points are raised. In all seriousness I should like to suggest to my hon. friends that a great deal of talk took place this afternoon and evening but I do not think anyone on the other side of the house addressed himself to the real issue before us, that is, whether or not the integration of the armed forces is the right policy for Canada. One would think that when this motion was presented they would use this opportunity to debate it intelligently, look at the real issues involved and not drag all sorts of red herrings across the scene. I hope they will use the balance of the available time for that purpose.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Greenwood.

Mr. Chairman, it may be disappointing to the members of the house but I have no newspaper or other gossip about what goes on in the smoke-filled back rooms of the Tory caucus to give to the house. I propose to discuss the issues of integration, unification and defence.

Hear, hear.

October 31. 1966
Interim Supply

The minister has expressed his disappointment at the remarks of other hon. members of the opposition. He has said he will speak again in the debate and I hope he will deal with the problems I intend to raise.
In the earlier part of his speech which he read to the house the minister made some statements about representative witnesses giving evidence before a committee. A part of this statement, if adopted, would completely undermine the confidence of any committee in the integrity of evidence given before it. I will deal later with this matter. At the moment, however, I should like to deal with what I think is the main issue. I should like to join with and support the protest already raised by members of the official opposition against the continued and obstinate refusal of the Minister of National Defence and the government he represents to allow the committee on national defence to review adequately the merits of the unification proposals-
Hear, hear.

-before parliament is asked to give its approval in principle on second reading. In his remarks the minister boasted about how willing he had been that the committee should have the facts before it. In so far as he has done that in the past, I give him every credit, but I challenge him to let the committee on national defence have the opportunity to hear not just one side of the case from the minister and his representative witnesses but also to hear from that body of persons who happen to disagree with the minister so that when we are asked in this house to debate the principle of unification we shall not be doing so on the basis of a one-sided story produced by the minister. I think we should be in a position to deal with this very complicated matter after hearing from those-I will deal with them in more detail later-who express their unhappiness and disquiet about it. I say it would be absolutely unforgivable and indefensible if this house were asked to commit itself to this very important principle of unification, which the minister himself has described as a fundamental re-organization, before the views of qualified and experienced persons have been expressed. People have expressed very grave reservations about some of these proposals.
People who have spent their lives in distinguished careers in the armed services have warned that in their judgment the course proposed by the government may destroy the

effectiveness of our armed services. I do not say that that is either right or wrong. Indeed, so far as I am concerned, if certain conditions were met, I think I might be inclined personally to be prejudiced in favour of the minister's proposals for integration. I say, however, that to proceed without a full hearing of the viewpoint expressed by these men prior to second reading would be irresponsible; in fact, it would be playing fast and loose with questions which affect the national security of this country.
Hear, hear.

Who are the men who have expressed their doubts? So far as the army is concerned, some of Canada's most distinguished soldiers have expressed their views. Two former chiefs of staff, General Foulkes and General Simonds, who supported the original idea of integration, have publicly expressed the view that unification as proposed by the minister is going too far. The same view has been expressed by Major General Volkes publicly. Brigadier R. S. Malone, according to the Winnipeg Free Press; has published a pamphlet entitled "Defence Forces Integration". He refers to the defence forces integration as a progressive step, and personally I am inclined to agree with him. He goes on, however, to say "this progressive step could be destroyed by two cardinal errors". Is parliament to be asked to give consideration in principle to proposals which such an informed and distinguished person as Brigadier Malone has described as cardinal errors?
On the side of the navy we have the contrary views of Admirals Landymore and Brock. Both have expressed the view that unification as at present proposed by the minister will seriously undermine or has already seriously undermined morale and contributed-I use the unexpurgated version of Admiral Landymore's words-to a desperate shortage of naval personnel required to meet commitments. I do not know whether Admiral Landymore is right, but as I say he should be heard again and be able to tell the committee, now that he has resigned or has been dismissed from the armed services, precisely what is the basis for this particular view.
October 31, 1966

The Halifax Chronicle-Herald of September 14 published another statement which is taken from a Canadian Press dispatch by Dave McIntosh. I should like to read it:
Sources close to the minister say he is inclined to regard as disloyal any officer who opposes unification on technical grounds-and that is where the main opposition lies.
I do not know who the source close to the minister is, but I presume he is close enough to the minister that he understands the minister's thinking. Apparently the minister regards as disloyal anyone who on technical grounds objects to unification. The dispatch continues:
This makes it awkward for staff officers who are supposed to give frank advice.
It was in such circumstances that three of the top five officers in the defence department lost their jobs in July. The dispatch further states:
Lt. Gen. Robert Moncel, vice chief of staff, Lt. Gen. Frank Fleury, comptroller-general, and Vice Admiral Kenneth Dyer, chief of personnel, advised Mr. Hellyer, after a careful study of unification to slow down the process.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Mr. Hellyer asked for and got their immediate resignations.
I do not know whether that is a correct statement, but-
Would the hon. member permit me to say that I have denied that categorically.
I do not know which part was denied categorically. Does the minister deny categorically that there was a careful study of unification made and a suggestion to slow down the process?
There was no paper advising a slowing down.

Was there a verbal statement made? The minister says there was no written statement or verbal statement and I accept his word, but I should like to know what Lt. Gen. Robert Moncel, Lt. Gen. Frank Fleury and Vice Admiral Kenneth Dyer would say about this issue. I would like to find out what they think about this process of unification and I should like to know why they retired before their normal time.
These are the sort of things this house and the committee of this house set up to look into these matters ought to know before the question of unification is presented to us. I do not know whether a careful study was made,
Interim Supply
but if one was made it has never been presented to the defence committee or to this house. I presume that careful studies have been made and I suggest that before this house is asked to deal with this complex and vital matter affecting the security of the country and the future usefulness of our armed services the committee set up for this purpose should hear both sides. I say to the minster and the house that so far the defence committee has only been allowed to hear one side.
In the early days of the defence committee, and I give the minister credit for this, we heard not only from the minister himself, from chiefs of staff and other officials but in addition we heard the views of retired officers such as General Foulkes and General Simonds who adopted a highly critical view about what was being done. We also heard from various outside independent critics.
At later sittings of the defence committee, and I want to point this out to the committee of the whole house, we did not hear from anybody except those who the minister said were in a representative capacity and to a degree which he himself has said, under the control and supervision of the defence department itself. I for one as a member of that defence committee believe it would be irresponsible to ask this house to deal with so complex an issue without permitting the committee and this house to hear from those who have expressed, after a lifetime of distinguished service, very grave doubts about the proposal of the minister.
What is the hurry in so far as unification is concerned? The minister has said that this is something novel which all nations should look at and regard. The minister has praised his own achievements to the sky, or at least his public relations officials have done so for him. Perhaps he is right. But if his proposals are so good why can he not wait a little while so that we can hear from the critics in a forum of this house where members can determine whether or not their criticism is valid.
The estimates of the department, as hon. members know, were rammed through by a majority of government members. I hope we are not going to have a change in the set-up of committees and that committees are not going to hear just official witnesses and then hear a government majority say: That is all; we will now report. I hope we will have committees which will truly weigh all sides of the question and produce somethin 1 useful.

October 31, 1966
Interim, Supply
In the early part of the minister's statement he read us some learned dissertations about the functions of representative witnesses. As a background to my statement I should like to read from the report of a select committee on witnesses which reported to the British House of Commons on May 9, 1935. Paragraph 8 of that report states:
Your committee think it of great importance to emphasize this. Whatever may be the character of a committee, whatever may be the nature of the evidence to be tendered by a witness, any interference with a witness's freedom is a breach of the privileges of the House of Commons.
The minister speaks about witnesses appearing in a representative capacity. I do not know whether he thinks that as a businessman he can tell these witnesses what to say, but I want the minister to pay attention to this part of the report:
A witness who is to give evidence in a representative capacity must, of course, consult beforehand with those whom he is to represent: and, apart from this, any witness may properly ask advice before giving evidence before any committee. Such advice may properly take the form of suggestions as to how he can best marshal his facts, no less than as to how he can best state his opinions, or the opinions of those on whose behalf he is speaking; but it is as improper for his adviser to interfere with his opinions, whether individual or representative, as to interfere with his facts.
I suggest that any interference with a witness before a committee of this house which takes the form of not just suggestions as to how he can best express himself but specifically urging him to change what he is going to say to the committee is a breach of the privileges of this house.
What are we to make of the memorandum that has now been produced as to the variations which were made? The minister says that so far as he knows the admiral did not object to these changes. I think that makes very little difference. A witness has been tampered with and whether or not he acquiesces makes no difference at all.
What is the difference between the two versions? I suggest that in discussing manpower the admiral expressed views on a matter of fact, peculiarly within his knowledge, which were watered down to the point of material suppression. Let us consider the words of Admiral Landymore dealing with manpower as contained in the unexpurgated version:
-I would like now to turn to my most valuable asset-manpower. This is the area of my greatest concern today because I am desperately short of the naval personnel required to meet my commitments.

As a member of the committee hearing those words I would have regarded that as a very strong warning to the committee that in the view of the admiral we were running into serious trouble in meeting our commitments. How does this statement appear in the expurgated version? It reads as follows:
This is the area of my greatest concern today because I am experiencing a shortage of the naval personnel to meet my immediate commitments.
The desperate nature of his concern is suppressed and the commitments are changed to immediate ones. So far as I an concerned, whether or not the minister chooses to call committee meetings or allow his officers to give evidence is one thing, but if they do give evidence and they do express in the drafts that they have prepared serious warnings to the members of the committee about matters of fact peculiarly within their knowledge, that is another thing. Who knew the situation better than Admiral Landymore? Yet because his knowledge perhaps reflected on policies of the minister-possibly it was through no fault of the minister that there was a desperately serious situation involving a shortage of naval personnel required to meet naval commitments-his brief was changed. I say that the committee and through it this house was entitled to the unexpurgated warning which the admiral wanted to give when he gave evidence on this occasion.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The minister has suggested to us that we did not discuss the issue of unification, and that is perfectly true. I do not think anybody has dealt with it very directly, but I would like to say a few words about it. I do not wish to suggest that either I or any member of this party is committed to opposition to the minister's proposal for integration. In fact, I am inclined to believe from what I do know that it may be a very important and worthwhile step forward. But I say to the minister that the time has come for him to explain clearly why this is necessary. It is not good enough to go on repeating that it is going to save us money. Of course we are all in favour of saving money; every rationalization saves money and this is the minister's duty. To the extent that he does it we commend him for it.
But the minister himself said that this proposal of unification is a fundamental reorganization, and the basic question has never been answered by him at all. From this I do not exclude the white paper. We have not been told what is the role of the Canadian forces and what they will be supposed to do.
October 31. 1966

I suggest that it is absolutely impossible for anyone to form an intelligent judgment about whether or not we should have unification until we are told what particular functions the minister and his government envisage the armed forces being called upon to perform. I say to the minister that if he came out boldly and said: "We are giving up some of these particular roles we have had in the past because they are now obsolete and we are going into a special role for Canada which will involve a unified operation and for this purpose integration would add to efficiency", he might get the enthusiastic support of the people of Canada, of the armed services and certainly of some of the members of this party. But he has not said so. Indeed, the government, typically has faced both ways.
At one time it was suggested we were going to phase out of the roles we occupy in NATO, reduce our brigade, our division, our anti-submarine forces, and our Bomarc missile active defence against air attack. The minister suggested in his vague way that maybe we will concentrate on a new role for Canada. He has completely failed to lift one little finger to change the present role of the armed services.
When this government was first elected three years ago, and even before it was elected, we heard that we were going to have a bold new policy and that the government would review the role of the Canadian armed services. We then had the white paper on defence which implied that some of these roles were obsolete, but we have never suggested it to our allies. At the present time, when the British, the Germans and the Americans are discussing a new approach to the problems of the military defence of Europe, we do not even hear a whimper from this government about any change it proposes to make. I suggest that as long as we carry out an isolated role integration makes no sense at all. If we are going to have a brigade of the army, as we have in the forward defences in Germany with the air support of the British and supplies which mainly come from the U.S. forces, and if at the same time we are to have a completely separate role carried out by the R.C.A.F. as another contribution, if we are to continue our anti-submarine role which is primarily the role of the navy although the air force may be partially concerned with it, and if we are to have a continued active defence through Bomarc
Interim Supply
missiles to prevent what I think is an obsolete and non-existent threat of a bomber attack, then we will have four or five isolated functions each of them performed by a separate service.
I suggest that to talk of integration in these circumstances is to talk nonsense. I say to the minister that he should give up all this press publicity about what a wonderful idea integration is. He should first of all tell parliament through the committee precisely what is planned and what it will involve. Second, he should tell the people of Canada through this parliament what it is all about. Third, he should make it clear to the armed services.
I cannot believe that the retirement of all these officers before their time is simply due to their desire to get out of the services early or through some obstinate resistance to change. I believe that if the minister will take the people of Canada into his confidence and produce a role for the armed services that makes sense, if he will say that to carry out this role effectively we need the integration of our services and this is how we will carry it out, he may get a great deal of support. The time has come for us to go behind the grandiose talk about how many millions of dollars have been saved, which has never been demonstrated to anybody's satisfaction, and get down to fundamentals. We want to know how our Canadian forces will be used and how the proposed integration will fit into the roles which will in fact be performed by those forces.
I conclude by saying to the minister once again that it would be irresponsible and unforgivable if he tried, in his enthusiasm for his own particular plans and for getting his own way, to force a majority in this House of Commons-no doubt the loyal backbenchers of his party will support him-to support his plan before any real opportunity has been given to the numerous qualified people who have given their lives to the services to point out before the committee just what are their reasons for their fears and apprehensions.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few introductory remarks which I will make tonight and tomorrow I will follow with a real speech. However, in the one minute left to us may I just say that the minister has told us he has reduced the forces by 23,000 men, he has saved $150 million, and now our forces are more effective than they have ever been in the past. Next year he can drop another

That sums up the ridiculousness of the minister's statement to us tonight, and tomorrow I will deal with some of the other nonsensical remarks that he made. I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.
Mr. Speaker, I presume we will carry on tomorrow with interim supply and the intensive study of defence.

Mr. Speaker, the government proposes to continue with interim supply. Later in the day we will call Item No. 101, second reading of Bill C-241, to be followed by Item No. 93, the resolution dealing with the Export Credits Insurance Act.

INDUSTRY-ONTARIO-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON BOYCOTT OF SUPERMARKETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 11 I asked the following question of the Prime Minister as reported at page 8514 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, In the absence of the Registrar General I would like to ask the Prime Minister if he can give us a report on the housewives' boycott of the supermarkets in Ontario.
The Prime Minister replied:
No, Mr. Speaker, I am not in a position to do that now, but I am following this boycott very carefully.
I presume that the Prime Minister is still following the boycott because he has not yet returned to tell us about what he has discovered. In the meantime I have been taking steps to find out something about this boycott which began in the city of Ottawa in the province of Ontario. I now find that it has become a Canada-wide protest which is growing as the days go by. The original Ottawa Consumers Protest Association is now in contact with similar groups in many Ontario cities and towns from Toronto down in size. It is in contact with Inflation Fighters, a large group in Montreal, with groups in the maritimes, in Calgary and in other prairie
(Mr. Churchill.]

points. Finally, no later than this afternoon they were in contact with the Vancouver "WASPS", which does not stand for what you might think but for "Women Against Soaring Prices". WASP is a very well chosen name, I think, and certainly will sting.
The boycotting of supermarkets is spreading geographically. As a matter of fact, it is not confined to Canada. During the past two weeks I have been in the United States and daily boycotting has been making the headlines of the New York papers and the front page of the New York Times on a number of occasions. Pictures of women boycotting supermarkets have been appearing practically every day. The boycott is spreading geographically and it is lengthening time-wise. This is the fourth week in which the women are maintaining their protests in Canada, and their numbers are considerable. I have been informed by the Ottawa group that they can count on something in the neighbourhood of two-thirds of the women in Ottawa to go into supermarkets only for certain items which have come down in price or are bargains. Otherwise they will stay away altogether. Very large numbers are affected.
Why are the women doing this? They are doing it for two reasons, to protest against the soaring price of food and to get the government to realize that they are in earnest and that something must be done about it. This is no fancy movement, Mr. Speaker. They feel that the price of basic food is spiralling out of range and that they must do something about it in the meantime by way of protest. But this has to be followed by government action.
I have heard a great deal said to the effect that women should not be bothering about the business of food, that other things such as medical costs, rents, steel and other segments of industry are equally important. But our women are deeply concerned about food prices and a large number of people on modest incomes as well as on very low incomes are affected. Welfare workers in this city have told these women that they are concerned, not only in this city but across Canada, about the serious way in which rising prices are affecting the nutrition of people. No one is starving but people are becoming seriously undernourished, and the next generation is going to run up medical bills of a very serious nature unless something is done to deal with the price of basic foodstuffs and to regard the matter as a major national problem at this time.
October 31, 1966

According to the report I received from the boycotting housewives, the supermarkets are now feeling the pinch and have come back fighting. They are trying all kinds of devices to buy off the women or to frighten them by understocking their shelves. They are trying to get them away from the boycott by putting certain articles on sale at bargain prices. They advertise bread at two loaves for 31 cents. The usual price is two for 39 cents. Women go in thinking they will get bargains only to find that the bread is stale and has not been moved from the day before.
This is not having the effect of discouraging women. Instead it is making them angry. Next week they are to go in for a selective boycott. They will begin next week by boycotting those household articles which have gimmicks attached. I speak of things like cereals with toys inside, packages of soap flakes and detergent with towels inside, jams with spoons attached, and so on.
In the face of this sort of thing the government should realize that action needs to be taken. This situation should be treated seriously and there should be a policy to deal with it. I am going to suggest a few things that the government should give its attention to. It should look into these things without waiting for the committee which is investigating prices to come up with anything, because that is not good enough.
I suggest that the government should consider now, as an immediate step, a freeze on the price of basic foods. I know that constitutional difficulties will be trotted out, but I know there are ways and means of dealing with premiers and getting constitutional matters settled because I have seen that done over the last numbers of years when the government wanted to do something.
Second, I believe that old age pensions, veterans pensions and family allowances must be brought up now to meet the presently spiralling prices. For the last few months these allowances have not been adequate to cope with the rising cost of living. This also is something which cannot wait for the leisurely investigation by the committee reviewing prices.
Third, I believe that trading stamps and gimmicks should be abolished. Fourth-I have only six points so I will be brief -legislation should be passed to limit the allowable deductions for advertising. Fifth, we should establish a department of consumer affairs with a prices review board as a watchdog on prices, with the authority to roll

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion back prices where they are unjustified. Sixth, the government should consider providing legislation to encourage co-operatives. All these suggestions should be given immediate attention in the face of the boycott situation.

I found prices down there fantastically high; the difference was notable even since I was there earlier. And I saw a new little trick. maintopic: HOUSING-REQUEST FOR REDUCED RENTALS IN PUBLIC HOUSING
HOUSING-REQUEST FOR REDUCED RENTALS IN PUBLIC HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in raising the question of the rental scales imposed on public housing in the city of
October 31. 1966

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Windsor I think I am bringing to the attention of this house a matter which is of great concern to the entire community. In doing so perhaps I might be permitted to say I think I am speaking for the industrial workers of Windsor and their families.
As the house knows, the economic rebirth of Windsor over the past few years has brought with it a serious housing shortage. This government, in co-operation with the provincial and municipal authorities, has done much to help deal with the shortage, but it still remains. This means that accommodation which would ordinarily be available for people earning income in excess of certain amounts who would otherwise not wish to live in public housing is almost not available at all, with the result that many industrial workers in Windsor are forced to pay the top penalty rate in the rental housing scale used in public housing in the city of Windsor.
They have little opportunity to seek accommodation in the private market because such accommodation is either not available to them at all or, if it is, the rents are, frankly, often exorbitant. I therefore felt it would be useful, as long ago as last February, to take up with the federal minister responsible for housing matters the question of adjusting downward the upper levels of these rental scales in a way which would be more realistic and take into account the wages presently earned by industrial workers in Windsor and the housing situation there.
I brought this matter again to the minister's attention this summer and again in September. On these latter occasions I was assured that the matter was under consideration in consultation with the Ontario Housing Corporation. I had hoped that this question might be decided at a recent board meeting of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I must say I was disappointed to find that this decision to reduce the upper levels in these rental scales had not been taken.
I think the situation could be summarized by reading a resolution which I received the other day from the Windsor city council adopting a resolution of Local 444 of the United Automobile Workers. It reads:
Whereas housing accommodation is a matter of great concern to the people of our community, and Whereas even when such accommodation is physically available, it is often made totally prohibitive because of the exorbitant rents asked, and Whereas while we welcome the geared-to-in-come accommodation now being provided, we must strongly object to the exceptionally high percentage of income called for under the present provisions, and

Whereas this prices these homes beyond the means of many, while extracting an unfair proportion of income from those who rent this accommodation,
Therefore, we urge that the maximum percentage called for be reduced from the present 31.8 to 25 per cent of income, and that city council quickly renew its application to the Ontario Housing Corporation and Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that this be done, emphasizing the urgency of this matter so that a fairer rent program can be implemented as soon as possible.
As the Windsor Star put it in an editorial on October 27:
Whether the federal officials like it or not the rentals now being charged-
This refers to public housing.
-are beyond the capabilities of the industrial worker to pay. The majority of these workers fall within the maximum percentage of 31.8 per cent of their income, and rents in the majority of cases exceed $150 monthly for families.
The editorial went on to say:
-it should be realized the purpose of government housing is defeated unless rents are within the reach of the industrial worker with a family.
At the request of the mayor and city council of Windsor I have arranged a meeting with the minister for Thursday, November 10th, so that we may go into this matter again. At this time, Mr. Speaker, I urge the parliamentary secretary to take back to the minister these points which I have also raised with him previously in writing and in person with respect to the need for a favourable decision as quickly as possible on this matter which is vital to the city of Windsor and its people.

speakeroldname: Mr. B. S. Mackasey (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: HOUSING-REQUEST FOR REDUCED RENTALS IN PUBLIC HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very hard not to take account of the excellent summary just presented by the hon. member from Windsor. He and I have often discussed this particular problem which is very acute in Windsor due to the tremendous success of the recent automotive pact which, according to the hon. member, has resulted in thousands of people flowing into the Windsor area to take advantage of the increased industrial production and increased number of jobs available in the community.
This, of course, has given rise to the problem which the hon. member has brought to the attention of the house in such an eloquent fashion, namely, that there is a distinct shortage of housing for the workers in the Windsor area and, because of this shortage,

the ever present danger of speculation, particularly in areas of old housing which are not under some type of control.
It may be of interest in passing to mention that in my own community of Verdun we still have rent controls in force which were imposed during the last war and which, for some unaccountable reason, and I am happy to say it, have not been removed. I do not know if it is the last such community in Canada but perhaps this would be a solution in an area like Windsor.
The hon. member has taken up this matter at considerable length, both verbally and in correspondence with the minister, but in all fairness to the minister and to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation I should point out that no formal request has been made by the Ontario Housing Corporation to C.M.H.C. It is true that there have been informal talks between the Ontario Housing Corporation and members of C.M.H.C. but, until the Ontario corporation makes a formal application to C.M.H.C. for a reduction of rentals, because of the complex federal-municipal arrangements we have in Canada the federal government cannot walk into Windsor and reduce rents. It must first receive a formal request from the Ontario Housing Corporation.
While the hon. member is perfectly right in approaching the minister and drawing the whole matter to the attention of C.M.H.C., I think it must be pointed out that similar eloquent pressure must be put on the Ontario Housing Corporation to the end that both bodies concerned with the problem may sit down and do something about it. However, Mr. Speaker, no later than tomorrow morning I shall draw the hon. member's remarks to the attention of the minister.

BROADCASTING-PRIORITY TO EDUCATIONAL NEEDS IN HIGH FREQUENCY CHANNEL ALLOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 27, as recorded at page 9168 of Hansard, I asked the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) this question:
As the minister knows, the Board of Broadcast Governors has just concluded two days of hearings on the future use of high frequency broadcasting bands in Canada. Is it the government's policy to give priority to educational broadcasting when the high frequency channels are allocated? I ask this question because some private broadcasters have been making applications.
9361
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
There is a small omission in the question as printed in Hansard because it should read ultra high frequency broadcasting bands.
One of the subjects which the B.B.G. dealt with at its hearings last week was the opening up of u.h.f. bands for television broadcasting. At the present time all television is carried on a very high frequency band which can only provide channels 2 to 13. It is further limited by international agreements. Canadian stations cannot interfere with American stations nearby, but the development of ultra high frequency broadcasting could greatly expand the available channels.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
I should also mention in passing that most television receiving sets in Canada cannot receive u.h.f. I have a question on the order paper about this. Manufacturers will need to make some changes in this connection. Appearing at the B.B.G. hearing on October 27 on the matter of educational broadcasting were representatives of the Ontario Department of Education, the Alberta Department of Education, the Nova Scotia Advisory Council on School Television, McGill University, the Metropolitan Educational T.V. Association of Toronto, the Ottawa Public School Board, the Metropolitan Edmonton Educational T.V. Association, the Canadian Home and School Parent-teacher Federation, the British Columbia School Trustees' Association, and the Ontario Federation of Home and School Associations. So there is great public interest.
At present educational television in Canada is very limited. The people who want to broacast educational programs have to fit in with the broadcasting schedules of the C.B.C. and private broadcasting stations. The latter have given pretty good co-operation and some very good programs have resulted. Not all the provinces have been given the use of this but to my knowledge Alberta, Ontario and Nova Scotia have done the best work in this field with the limited time available to them on the channels.
Is it the government's policy to give priority to educational broadcasting when the high frequency channels are allocated? I ask this question because some private interests appeared at the B.B.G. hearing to ask for some u.h.f. channels. One applicant proposed a third television broadcasting network for Canada using both v.h.f. and u.h.f. stations. I will not comment at this time on the question of whether or not this country can afford a third network. I want only an assurance that

It seems to me that in our large metropolitan areas more than one channel on the u.h.f. band will be required for educational broadcasting. I am thinking of cities like Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver. I am also thinking of what has to be done through the elementary and secondary schools, colleges and universities as well as the requirements of adult education. I am seeking an assurance from the government that educational television will have a priority over all other forms of broadcasting when the u.h.f. band is opened up.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very closely to the statement just made by the member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) in a commendable effort to get an answer to the question he put last Thursday to the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), and which was ruled out of order by the Chair.

The hon. member probably knows that the matter he raised comes under the Board of Broadcast Governors. As he mentioned when he put his question last week, the Board of Broadcast Governors met on October 25 and 26 and discussed, among other things, the future use of very high frequency broadcasting bands in Canada.
At those meetings, representatives of certain provinces and organizations were able to express their views freely and openly and to put forward all arguments in favour of giving priority to educational broadcasting when the very high frequency broadcasting bands will be allocated.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, and I think the hon. member will agree with me, the government will have to wait until the B.B.G. makes a ruling before it can decide on this matter. The hon. member is fully aware that the B.B.G. does not make its decisions on the spot and that sometimes we get the reports two or three weeks after the hearings.
